entries.meaning: To trouble or harass someone from every side at once; in older use, to surround or hem something in.
examples: Small delays beset every large construction job.
Doubts beset her the whole night before the interview.
The expedition has been beset by bad weather since Tuesday.
By March the project had been beset with lawsuits.
Wolves beset the camp on three sides that winter.
The travelers had been beset by bandits before they reached the pass.
A crown beset with rubies lay on the cushion.
The binding has been beset with small pearls along the spine.

senses.head: Trouble from every side
body: The living sense, and almost always passive — beset by delays, beset with problems. The trouble is the subject and the person or project it surrounds is the object. (осаждать, донимать, преследовать)
examples: Small delays beset every large construction job.
Doubts beset her the whole night before the interview.
The expedition has been beset by bad weather since Tuesday.
By March the project had been beset with lawsuits.

senses.head: Surround, hem in
body: The literal military sense — attackers closing in on all sides. Literary and largely archaic; modern American English says surround or besiege. (окружать, обступать)
examples: Wolves beset the camp on three sides that winter.
The travelers had been beset by bandits before they reached the pass.

senses.head: Stud, set thickly with
body: Very rare and poetic: a surface beset with jewels. You will meet it only in older texts and in translations that keep an old flavor. (усыпать, украшать (драгоценностями))
examples: A crown beset with rubies lay on the cushion.
The binding has been beset with small pearls along the spine.

entries.register: rare — met almost only in the passive beset by delays; few Americans produce it otherwise
entries.contrast: Almost always passive — beset by or beset with — so the participle is the form you actually meet: a project beset by delays. There is no besetted; it takes every form from set.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the beset by delays participle is so common that it works almost adjectivally, naming a condition rather than an event.
entries.transitivity: transitive in all three senses — the object is whatever the trouble surrounds (doubts beset her, wolves beset the camp). The object is obligatory: ✗ small delays beset.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the form you actually meet — the expedition has been beset by bad weather since Tuesday, a crown beset with rubies.

entries.meaning: To risk money on an outcome, or, in everyday speech, to say you are fairly sure of something.
examples: I never bet more than I can afford to lose.
He bet twenty dollars on the Sunday game and lost it.
She has bet on that same horse three years running.
I bet she's stuck in traffic again.
I'll bet he never even read the memo.
“Can you cover Friday?” “You bet.”
“Thanks for the ride.” “You bet.”
Don't bet on the weather holding through Sunday.
The whole plan had bet on interest rates staying low.

senses.head: Wager money on an outcome
body: The core sense: bet an amount on something, or bet someone that something will happen. American English keeps bet in the past and participle where British writing sometimes allows betted. (делать ставку, ставить деньги, биться об заклад)
examples: I never bet more than I can afford to lose.
He bet twenty dollars on the Sunday game and lost it.
She has bet on that same horse three years running.

senses.head: I bet — I'm fairly sure
body: Present tense even though it is the same shape as the past, and nearly always first person. Conversational, and often ironic — I bet you did. (держу пари, спорим, наверняка)
examples: I bet she's stuck in traffic again.
I'll bet he never even read the memo.

senses.head: You bet — certainly
body: A fixed spoken reply meaning “yes, definitely,” and across much of the U.S. also a casual “you're welcome.” Speech only. (конечно, ещё бы; не за что)
examples: “Can you cover Friday?” “You bet.”
“Thanks for the ride.” “You bet.”

senses.head: Bet on — rely on
body: Figurative: to treat an outcome as safe enough to plan around. Very often negative — don't bet on it, I wouldn't bet on him. (рассчитывать на, полагаться на)
examples: Don't bet on the weather holding through Sunday.
The whole plan had bet on interest rates staying low.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking, in money talk and in I bet
entries.contrast: American English keeps bet in the past — he bet fifty dollars — where British writing sometimes allows betted. Watch the other trap too: I bet meaning "I'm fairly sure" (I bet she's late) is present tense even though it is the same shape as the past.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the wagering sense; I bet she's late and you bet are fixed speech formulas, present tense despite looking like the past.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (I never bet), transitive (he bet twenty dollars), ditransitive (I'll bet you ten dollars), and it also takes a that-clause.
entries.passive: restricted — the money sense passivizes stiffly (a fortune was bet on that race), and the idioms have no passive at all: ✗ that she's late is bet by me.

entries.meaning: To send a program or signal out over radio, television, or the internet; more loosely, to tell something to everyone.
examples: The station broadcasts the local news at six.
NPR broadcast the hearings live all day Thursday.
That episode has been broadcast in forty countries.
Please don't broadcast my phone number to the whole office.
He broadcast the news before the family had been told.
We broadcast clover seed across the pasture in March.
The mix had been broadcast over the bare ground before the rain.

senses.head: Transmit a program
body: The main sense, for radio, TV, and streaming alike. Edited American prose keeps broadcast in all three slots; broadcasted is common in speech but most editors still change it. (передавать в эфир, транслировать, вещать)
examples: The station broadcasts the local news at six.
NPR broadcast the hearings live all day Thursday.
That episode has been broadcast in forty countries.

senses.head: Announce to everyone
body: Figurative and usually disapproving — spreading something widely that should have stayed private. (разглашать, раззвонить, трубить о)
examples: Please don't broadcast my phone number to the whole office.
He broadcast the news before the family had been told.

senses.head: Scatter seed by hand
body: The original agricultural sense — throwing seed widely instead of sowing it in rows — and the source of the radio meaning. Still current among farmers and gardeners. (разбрасывать (семена), сеять вразброс)
examples: We broadcast clover seed across the pasture in March.
The mix had been broadcast over the bare ground before the rain.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary for radio, TV, and streaming, and figuratively for spreading news
entries.contrast: Edited American prose keeps broadcast in all three slots — the game was broadcast live. Broadcasted turns up in casual and technical writing, but most editors still change it. Rebroadcast, telecast, and simulcast behave the same way.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from transmitting a program to scattering seed across a pasture.
entries.transitivity: both — normally transitive (NPR broadcast the hearings live), intransitive when the station itself is the subject (we broadcast from a studio downtown).
entries.passive: yes, and it is the everyday form — that episode has been broadcast in forty countries, the mix had been broadcast over the bare ground before the rain.

entries.meaning: To break open suddenly under pressure, or to move or act with sudden force.
examples: Balloons burst if you fill them too far.
Water pipes burst all over the city during the freeze last January.
Two of the tires have burst since we bought the trailer.
She burst into the room without knocking.
Three kids had burst out of the building before the alarm stopped.
He burst into tears in the middle of the ceremony.
That model has burst into flames twice on the highway.
He bursts out laughing every time he hears that song.
She burst out crying before she got through the first sentence.
The closets are bursting with things nobody uses.
He was bursting with news about the promotion.
She was bursting to tell someone the whole time.
I am bursting to ask him what really happened.

senses.head: Break open under pressure
body: Of pipes, balloons, tires, dams — anything that gives way all at once. There is no bursted, so the time word carries the tense. (лопаться, разрываться, прорываться)
examples: Balloons burst if you fill them too far.
Water pipes burst all over the city during the freeze last January.
Two of the tires have burst since we bought the trailer.

senses.head: Burst into — move suddenly
body: Sudden, forceful movement into or out of a place; the preposition carries the direction. (врываться, вылетать (откуда-л.))
examples: She burst into the room without knocking.
Three kids had burst out of the building before the alarm stopped.

senses.head: Burst into tears or flames
body: A fixed frame for something that starts all at once, with a noun after into. Burst into tears, burst into flames, and burst into song are the common ones. (разразиться (слезами), вспыхнуть, грянуть)
examples: He burst into tears in the middle of the ceremony.
That model has burst into flames twice on the highway.

senses.head: Burst out laughing / crying
body: The same idea with an -ing verb instead of a noun. Burst out also introduces sudden speech: “Enough!” he burst out. (расхохотаться, разрыдаться)
examples: He bursts out laughing every time he hears that song.
She burst out crying before she got through the first sentence.

senses.head: Be bursting with — overflowing
body: Progressive only, and usually figurative — bursting with pride, energy, or news. A closet can be bursting with clothes as well. (быть переполненным (чем-л.))
examples: The closets are bursting with things nobody uses.
He was bursting with news about the promotion.

senses.head: Be bursting to do something
body: Informal, progressive only, and always with an infinitive: barely able to hold back from doing something. (не терпеться (что-л. сделать))
examples: She was bursting to tell someone the whole time.
I am bursting to ask him what really happened.

entries.register: everyday — pipes, balloons, tears, and laughter all burst in ordinary speech
entries.contrast: There is no bursted. Because the past is identical to the present, the time word carries the tense: pipes burst every winter is a habit, the pipe burst last night is one event that is over.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and sudden throughout; be bursting with and be bursting to are progressive-only frames.
entries.transitivity: both, but overwhelmingly intransitive (the pipe burst, she burst into the room); transitive only in a narrow set — burst a balloon, burst a blood vessel.
entries.passive: restricted — the intransitive senses have no passive at all (✗ the room was burst into); the rare transitive allows a blood vessel was burst by the strain, but popped or broke reads better.
entries.phrasal verbs: burst in · burst into · burst out

entries.meaning: Informal: to break something, to raid or arrest, or to reduce someone in rank. Everyday American usage prefers the regular busted.
examples: Don't bust the lock — I have a key somewhere.
He bust his ankle skateboarding last summer.
Two of the hinges had bust clean off before we noticed.
My brother busted his phone screen again.
Vice has bust that club twice this year.
He got busted for driving without a license.
The colonel busted him to private for the stunt.
Two sergeants have been busted since the investigation opened.
They busted up over money after eleven years.
Somebody had busted up the picnic tables during the night.
He busted a gut getting the truck loaded before dark.
Don't bust my chops about the deadline — I know.

senses.head: Break, smash
body: Informal for break. American English usually says busted in the past and participle; the invariant bust sounds British or old-fashioned. In writing that matters, use broke. (сломать, разбить, расколотить)
examples: Don't bust the lock — I have a key somewhere.
He bust his ankle skateboarding last summer.
Two of the hinges had bust clean off before we noticed.
My brother busted his phone screen again.

senses.head: Raid or arrest (police)
body: Slang from law enforcement and crime reporting: police bust a club, or bust someone for something. Write raided or arrested in formal prose. (накрыть, арестовать, устроить облаву)
examples: Vice has bust that club twice this year.
He got busted for driving without a license.

senses.head: Demote in rank
body: Military and police usage, usually passive: he was busted to private. Always regular here. (разжаловать, понизить в звании)
examples: The colonel busted him to private for the stunt.
Two sergeants have been busted since the investigation opened.

senses.head: Bust up — break apart, brawl
body: Bust up a fight, a marriage, or the furniture; intransitively, a couple busts up. Informal throughout. (разгромить, разнести; поссориться, разойтись)
examples: They busted up over money after eleven years.
Somebody had busted up the picnic tables during the night.

senses.head: Bust a gut, bust chops
body: Set slangy phrases: bust a gut is to work or laugh very hard, and bust someone's chops is to nag or needle them. (надрываться, из кожи вон лезть; придираться, пилить)
examples: He busted a gut getting the truck loaded before dark.
Don't bust my chops about the deadline — I know.

entries.forms: bust /bʌst/ · bust /bʌst/ or busted /ˈbʌstɪd/ · bust /bʌst/ or busted /ˈbʌstɪd/
entries.register: everyday — informal, but wholly ordinary in American speech and crime reporting
entries.contrast: Informal in every sense, and the regular busted is the commoner American past and participle: the police busted him, my phone is busted. Invariant bust sounds more British. In writing that matters, use broke, arrested, or raided instead.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and informal throughout; the participle busted doubles as an adjective (my phone is busted).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the break, raid, and demote senses (they busted the lock, vice busted that club), intransitive of a couple in bust up (they busted up over money).
entries.passive: yes, and the get-passive is the commonest form — he got busted for driving without a license, two sergeants have been busted since the investigation opened.
entries.phrasal verbs: bust in · bust out · bust up

entries.meaning: To throw or send something out, to choose actors for parts, or to shape molten metal in a mold.
examples: They have cast an unknown actor as the lead.
The director had cast the whole film before the script was finished.
She casts mostly out of open auditions.
She cast the line into the shallow water and waited.
Learn to cast into the wind and you can fish anywhere.
Voters cast their ballots on Tuesday.
More than a million people have cast early votes this cycle.
The lamp casts a long shadow across the hallway.
The audit has cast doubt on every figure in the report.
He cast a quick glance at the door and kept talking.
Would you cast an eye over these numbers before I send them?
Don't cast the blame on people who weren't in the room.
The memo had cast suspicion on the wrong department.
The witch casts a spell that turns the prince to stone.
That coastline has cast a spell over painters for a century.
The bell was cast in a foundry outside Cincinnati.
They cast the replacement part in bronze last month.
We cast off at dawn and were out of the harbor by six.
He had cast aside every draft before the good one came.
She cast about for a polite way to say no.
The committee has cast around for a new chair since March.

senses.head: Choose actors for parts
body: The commonest modern sense: cast someone as a character, or cast a film as a whole. Never casted in edited prose — casted survives only as shop talk inside the industry. (распределять роли, проводить кастинг, утверждать на роль)
examples: They have cast an unknown actor as the lead.
The director had cast the whole film before the script was finished.
She casts mostly out of open auditions.

senses.head: Throw, cast a line
body: The old literal sense, alive in fishing (cast a line) and in writing with a formal flavor. Ordinary speech says throw. (бросать, кидать, забрасывать)
examples: She cast the line into the shallow water and waited.
Learn to cast into the wind and you can fish anywhere.

senses.head: Cast a vote or ballot
body: The fixed phrase for voting; cast a ballot and cast a vote are equally standard, and the news writes little else. (подавать голос, голосовать, опускать бюллетень)
examples: Voters cast their ballots on Tuesday.
More than a million people have cast early votes this cycle.

senses.head: Cast light, a shadow, doubt
body: A frame for whatever a thing projects, literal or figurative: cast a shadow, cast light on the problem, cast doubt on a claim. (отбрасывать (тень), проливать (свет), бросать тень сомнения)
examples: The lamp casts a long shadow across the hallway.
The audit has cast doubt on every figure in the report.

senses.head: Cast a glance or eye
body: A slightly formal way of saying look. Common in writing, rare in speech. (бросить взгляд, окинуть взглядом, просмотреть)
examples: He cast a quick glance at the door and kept talking.
Would you cast an eye over these numbers before I send them?

senses.head: Cast blame or suspicion
body: To direct blame, suspicion, or aspersions at someone. Formal, and a staple of reporting on scandals. (возлагать (вину), бросать тень (подозрения))
examples: Don't cast the blame on people who weren't in the room.
The memo had cast suspicion on the wrong department.

senses.head: Cast a spell
body: Fixed in magic and fantasy — cast a spell on someone. The figurative use follows easily: a place can cast a spell over you. (наводить чары, колдовать, заколдовывать)
examples: The witch casts a spell that turns the prince to stone.
That coastline has cast a spell over painters for a century.

senses.head: Cast metal in a mold
body: The foundry sense, and the source of cast iron and a plaster cast. Usually passive, and the participle often works as an adjective. (отливать (металл), формовать)
examples: The bell was cast in a foundry outside Cincinnati.
They cast the replacement part in bronze last month.

senses.head: Cast off / cast aside
body: Cast off is to untie a boat and, in knitting, to finish the last row; cast aside is to discard something or someone. Both are on the formal side. (отдавать швартовы; отбрасывать, отвергать)
examples: We cast off at dawn and were out of the harbor by six.
He had cast aside every draft before the good one came.

senses.head: Cast about / around for
body: To search for something intangible — an idea, an excuse, a replacement. Literary rather than spoken. (искать, подыскивать, ломать голову в поисках)
examples: She cast about for a polite way to say no.
The committee has cast around for a new chair since March.

entries.register: everyday — everyone casts a vote, a shadow, a line, or a show
entries.contrast: No -ed form: the film was cast in three weeks, never casted. Casted survives only as shop talk inside the entertainment industry. Every compound here — broadcast, forecast, recast, miscast, typecast, downcast — copies it exactly.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, literal and figurative alike; the participle is adjectival in cast iron.
entries.transitivity: both — overwhelmingly transitive (cast a ballot, cast an unknown actor as the lead); intransitive with a particle (we cast off at dawn, she cast about for a polite way to say no).
entries.passive: yes — the bell was cast in a foundry outside Cincinnati, the whole film had been cast before the script was finished.
entries.phrasal verbs: cast about · cast around · cast aside · cast away · cast down · cast off · cast on · cast out
entries.see also: broadcast, forecast, recast, miscast, typecast, telecast

entries.meaning: To log an area of forest by taking every tree at once.
examples: The company clear-cuts about a thousand acres a year.
Loggers clear-cut that ridge back in the 1970s.
Half the watershed has been clear-cut since the mill reopened.
The slope had been clear-cut long before the state bought it.
They plan to clear-cut the northern parcel next spring.

senses.head: Log every tree at once
body: A forestry term, and the only verb sense there is. The far commoner adjective clear-cut — a clear-cut case of fraud — is a separate word and never behaves like this verb. (вырубать лес сплошь, вести сплошную рубку)
examples: The company clear-cuts about a thousand acres a year.
Loggers clear-cut that ridge back in the 1970s.
Half the watershed has been clear-cut since the mill reopened.
The slope had been clear-cut long before the state bought it.
They plan to clear-cut the northern parcel next spring.

entries.register: rare — a forestry term; what Americans use daily is the unrelated adjective a clear-cut case
entries.contrast: The verb is far rarer than the adjective clear-cut meaning "obvious" — a clear-cut case of fraud. As a verb it takes its forms straight from cut.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and purely a forestry verb; the common adjective a clear-cut case of fraud is a separate word that never behaves like it.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the tract of forest (loggers clear-cut that ridge); it drops only when the practice itself is meant (the company clear-cuts about a thousand acres a year).
entries.passive: yes, and it is the usual form in reporting — half the watershed has been clear-cut since the mill reopened.

entries.meaning: To have a particular price, or to make someone lose something.
examples: A ticket costs about ninety dollars now.
Good tools cost money, but they last.
The repair cost more than the car was worth.
Rent has cost us more every year since we moved in.
That one mistake has cost us two customers already.
His temper cost him the promotion last year.
It cost her more than she let on to walk away.
Speaking up in that meeting had cost him every ally he had.
Parking downtown costs an arm and a leg on game days.
Getting the roof fixed cost us an arm and a leg.
The contractor costed the job at twelve thousand dollars.
We have costed out both options and the second is cheaper.

senses.head: Have a price
body: The core sense, invariant in all three forms: the repair cost four hundred dollars. Never costed here. (стоить)
examples: A ticket costs about ninety dollars now.
Good tools cost money, but they last.
The repair cost more than the car was worth.
Rent has cost us more every year since we moved in.

senses.head: Make someone lose something
body: The thing lost is the object and the person is the indirect object: it cost him the promotion. Money is not involved. (стоить (чего-л.), лишить, обойтись в)
examples: That one mistake has cost us two customers already.
His temper cost him the promotion last year.

senses.head: Take effort or sacrifice
body: Of effort rather than price: it cost her a great deal to say that. Slightly formal, and the object is usually an amount of pain or trouble. (даваться ценой, стоить усилий)
examples: It cost her more than she let on to walk away.
Speaking up in that meeting had cost him every ally he had.

senses.head: Cost a fortune
body: Fixed informal phrases for something expensive. That'll cost you is a joking price attached to a favor. (стоить целое состояние, влететь в копеечку)
examples: Parking downtown costs an arm and a leg on game days.
Getting the roof fixed cost us an arm and a leg.

senses.head: Work out a price (costed)
body: The one sense that is regular — costed, never invariant cost. Accounting and contracting writing only. (калькулировать, рассчитывать себестоимость)
examples: The contractor costed the job at twelve thousand dollars.
We have costed out both options and the second is cheaper.

entries.register: everyday — one of the first hundred verbs anyone uses
entries.contrast: Two verbs share this spelling. Meaning "have a price," it never changes: the repair cost four hundred dollars. Meaning "work out the price of something," it is regular: the contractor costed the job at $12,000. Only that second, accounting sense takes costed.
entries.verb type: stative in the price and loss senses — a property of the thing, not an act, and it rejects the progressive: ✗ the ticket is costing ninety dollars. Only the accounting sense (costed the job) is a true action verb.
entries.transitivity: transitive with an amount (the repair cost four hundred dollars), and ditransitive with the person first (it cost him the promotion, that mistake has cost us two customers).
entries.passive: no in the price and loss senses — ✗ four hundred dollars was cost by the repair, ✗ the promotion was cost him. Only the dynamic accounting sense passivizes: the job was costed at twelve thousand dollars.

entries.meaning: To cut across something — across the grain of a board, or between two scenes on film.
examples: You crosscut the board first, then rip it to width.
He crosscut the plank a quarter inch too short.
This blade crosscuts cleanly but tears the grain when you rip.
The editor has crosscut between the two conversations.
The director had crosscut the chase with shots of the empty house.
These loyalties crosscut every party line in the region.
The survey had crosscut the usual age brackets on purpose.

senses.head: Saw across the grain
body: Woodworking. A crosscut goes across the grain; ripping goes along it, and the tool for the first is a crosscut saw. (пилить поперёк волокон, делать поперечный распил)
examples: You crosscut the board first, then rip it to width.
He crosscut the plank a quarter inch too short.
This blade crosscuts cleanly but tears the grain when you rip.

senses.head: Alternate two scenes on film
body: Editing vocabulary, interchangeable with intercut. Usually crosscut between two lines of action. (монтировать параллельно, чередовать сцены)
examples: The editor has crosscut between the two conversations.
The director had crosscut the chase with shots of the empty house.

senses.head: Cut across, run counter to
body: Academic and policy writing, usually about loyalties or categories that ignore the usual dividing lines. The -ing form does most of the work — crosscutting concerns, crosscutting cleavages. (пересекать, идти вразрез, перекрывать границы)
examples: These loyalties crosscut every party line in the region.
The survey had crosscut the usual age brackets on purpose.

entries.register: rare — woodworking and film-editing shop talk, mostly met in crosscut saw
entries.contrast: Mostly technical — a saw cut across the grain, or a film that alternates between two scenes. Forms follow cut, and in the film sense it is interchangeable with intercut.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the -ing form has hardened into an adjective in policy writing (crosscutting concerns, crosscutting cleavages).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive on a board, a scene, or a set of categories (he crosscut the plank, these loyalties crosscut every party line), intransitive of how a tool behaves and in crosscut between two conversations.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the chase had been crosscut with shots of the empty house.

entries.meaning: To divide or wound with something sharp, to reduce an amount, and, in a long list of fixed phrases, to stop, shorten, or remove.
examples: Please cut the bread into thick slices.
She cut the rope with a pocketknife.
Someone has cut the cake already.
I cut my finger on the lid this morning.
He had cut his hand on the broken glass before anyone noticed.
Airlines cut fares whenever a new route opens.
The state cut funding before anyone was told.
They have cut the budget twice since June.
She cuts everyone's hair in the family.
He cut his own hair during the lockdown and it showed.
We cut the trip short because of the storm.
The editor has cut the chapter down to four pages.
He cut class three times last week.
Nobody has cut a shift since the new schedule went up.
She cut me off before I finished the sentence.
The storm had cut off the whole valley by morning.
Cut it out — people are trying to sleep.
The motor cut out halfway across the lake.
They have cut two songs out of the set list.
I have cut down on coffee since the checkup.
They cut down the old maple last fall.
A pickup cut in front of us on the ramp.
Somebody has cut in line ahead of forty people.
The two sides cut a deal an hour before the deadline.
Accounting has cut the check already.

senses.head: Divide with a blade
body: The literal sense — knife, scissors, saw. Usually with a phrase saying how: cut it into slices, cut it in half. Never cutted. (резать, разрезать, нарезать)
examples: Please cut the bread into thick slices.
She cut the rope with a pocketknife.
Someone has cut the cake already.

senses.head: Wound with something sharp
body: Transitive and often reflexive, with a body part as object: I cut my finger. The participle doubles as an adjective — a cut lip. (порезать(ся), поранить)
examples: I cut my finger on the lid this morning.
He had cut his hand on the broken glass before anyone noticed.

senses.head: Reduce an amount
body: Of budgets, prices, staff, taxes, and emissions. One of the most common verbs in business and political news. (сокращать, урезать, снижать)
examples: Airlines cut fares whenever a new route opens.
The state cut funding before anyone was told.
They have cut the budget twice since June.

senses.head: Cut hair
body: Cut someone's hair, or, for what you had done to you, the passive — I got my hair cut. (стричь)
examples: She cuts everyone's hair in the family.
He cut his own hair during the lockdown and it showed.

senses.head: Shorten, trim down
body: Taking material out of something: cut a scene, cut two pages, cut a trip short. (сокращать (текст), урезать, обрывать)
examples: We cut the trip short because of the storm.
The editor has cut the chapter down to four pages.

senses.head: Skip class or work
body: American school and workplace slang: cut class, cut school, cut a shift. British English says skive. (прогуливать)
examples: He cut class three times last week.
Nobody has cut a shift since the new schedule went up.

senses.head: Cut off — interrupt, disconnect, isolate
body: Three related uses: interrupting a speaker, ending a supply, and leaving a place unreachable. Cut someone off in traffic is a fourth. (перебивать; отключать; отрезать (от мира))
examples: She cut me off before I finished the sentence.
The storm had cut off the whole valley by morning.

senses.head: Cut out — stop, remove
body: Cut it out means stop that; cut out a picture is to remove it; an engine that cuts out dies suddenly. (прекратить; вырезать; заглохнуть)
examples: Cut it out — people are trying to sleep.
The motor cut out halfway across the lake.
They have cut two songs out of the set list.

senses.head: Cut down (on) — reduce; fell
body: Cut down on something is to consume less of it; cut down a tree is to fell it. The object decides which you mean. (сокращать (потребление); срубить)
examples: I have cut down on coffee since the checkup.
They cut down the old maple last fall.

senses.head: Cut in — interrupt, overtake
body: Cut in line, cut in on a conversation, or cut in on a car. Separately, cut someone in on a deal is to give them a share. (вмешаться, влезть без очереди, подрезать)
examples: A pickup cut in front of us on the ramp.
Somebody has cut in line ahead of forty people.

senses.head: Cut a deal or check
body: Fixed American phrases where cut simply means make. Cut a check is standard business usage for issuing a payment. (заключить сделку; выписать чек; записать пластинку)
examples: The two sides cut a deal an hour before the deadline.
Accounting has cut the check already.

entries.register: everyday — among the commonest verbs in the language, literal and figurative alike
entries.contrast: Never cutted. Every compound in this file — undercut, intercut, uppercut, crosscut, clear-cut — copies it without change.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, literal and figurative; the participle serves as an adjective in a cut lip.
entries.transitivity: both — normally transitive (she cut the rope, they cut the budget twice), intransitive of an engine or a person moving in (the motor cut out, a pickup cut in front of us).
entries.passive: yes — the chapter has been cut down to four pages, the whole valley had been cut off by morning, I got my hair cut.
entries.phrasal verbs: cut across · cut away · cut back · cut back on · cut down · cut down on · cut in · cut into · cut loose · cut off · cut out · cut through · cut up
entries.see also: undercut, intercut, uppercut, crosscut, clear-cut, split

entries.meaning: To turn the eyes downward, or to dishearten someone. Literary and rare as a verb; the adjective downcast is what you normally meet.
examples: She has downcast her eyes every time the subject comes up.
He had downcast his gaze before the judge finished speaking.
Long winters downcast the spirits of everyone on the island.
The news from the mill downcast the whole town that spring.
The verdict downcast everyone who had worked on the case.
Nothing downcasts a crew faster than a canceled contract.

senses.head: Lower the eyes
body: The eyes or the gaze are almost the only possible object. In practice the participle-adjective carries the meaning — downcast eyes — and the verb itself is archaic. (опускать (глаза, взгляд))
examples: She has downcast her eyes every time the subject comes up.
He had downcast his gaze before the judge finished speaking.

senses.head: Dishearten, depress
body: Literary and old-fashioned. Ordinary American English says discourage or depress. (удручать, подавлять, повергать в уныние)
examples: Long winters downcast the spirits of everyone on the island.
The news from the mill downcast the whole town that spring.
The verdict downcast everyone who had worked on the case.
Nothing downcasts a crew faster than a canceled contract.

entries.register: archaic — the verb is out of use; only the participle-adjective downcast eyes survives
entries.contrast: You will meet this almost only as an adjective — downcast eyes, he looked downcast. As a verb it is literary and old-fashioned; ordinary American English says discourage or depress. Forms follow cast.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, but archaic as a verb; in living English downcast is a participle-adjective (downcast eyes, he looked downcast).
entries.transitivity: transitive in both senses — the object is the eyes or the person dispirited (she downcast her eyes, the verdict downcast everyone).
entries.passive: restricted — a passive is buildable (the whole town was downcast by the news) but reads as the adjective; modern American English says was discouraged or was depressed.

entries.meaning: To translate something into English. Rare, dated, and written with a small e to keep it apart from the name of the language.
examples: Only a handful of scholars english Old Norse sagas today.
It is hard to english a joke that depends on grammar.
In 1611 a royal committee englished the Hebrew scriptures.
Nobody has englished that poet's late work yet.
By 1700 printers had englished most of the popular French romances.

senses.head: Translate into English
body: A scholar's word, mostly historical — a royal committee englished the scriptures. Modern American English uses the regular englished when it uses the word at all, and normally just says translated into English. The english of pool and billiards, meaning spin on the ball, is an unrelated noun. (переводить на английский язык)
examples: Only a handful of scholars english Old Norse sagas today.
It is hard to english a joke that depends on grammar.
In 1611 a royal committee englished the Hebrew scriptures.
Nobody has englished that poet's late work yet.
By 1700 printers had englished most of the popular French romances.

entries.forms: english /ˈɪŋɡlɪʃ/ · english /ˈɪŋɡlɪʃ/ or englished /ˈɪŋɡlɪʃt/ · english /ˈɪŋɡlɪʃ/ or englished /ˈɪŋɡlɪʃt/
entries.register: archaic — a scholar's word for translating, at home in older writing and nowhere else
entries.third person: englishes · -ing form: englishing (the third person adds -es after -sh)
entries.contrast: A rare, dated verb, written with a small e to keep it apart from the name of the language. Modern American English uses the regular englished when it uses the word at all, and normally just says translated into English. The unrelated english of pool and billiards — spin on the ball — is a noun, not a verb.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and archaic: a scholar's word for the act of translating, written with a small e.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the text being translated (english the Old Norse sagas), and it is obligatory.
entries.passive: yes — most of the popular French romances had been englished by 1700 — though a modern writer would say translated into English.

entries.meaning: To be the right size or shape for something, to make something the right size, or to suit and belong.
examples: These jeans fit better than the last pair.
The key fit the lock on the first try.
Nothing in that closet has fit me since high school.
That story fits everything else we know.
The description fit the man they arrested.
Six people fit in that car if nobody has luggage.
The couch had fit through the door on the way in, somehow.
They fitted the whole floor with new smoke alarms.
The van has been fitted with a lift.
The tailor fitted the jacket in twenty minutes.
She has been fitted for a brace twice this year.
He never fit in at that school.
New hires fit in faster when someone shows them around.
The dentist fit me in at four.
She has fit two more meetings into an already full day.

senses.head: Be the right size
body: The core sense, and the one that keeps the invariant fit in the American past and participle: the jacket fit me perfectly last year. (быть впору, подходить по размеру)
examples: These jeans fit better than the last pair.
The key fit the lock on the first try.
Nothing in that closet has fit me since high school.

senses.head: Suit, be consistent with
body: Figurative: a story fits the facts, a person fits the job, a punishment fits the crime. (соответствовать, подходить, вязаться с)
examples: That story fits everything else we know.
The description fit the man they arrested.

senses.head: Go into a space
body: Intransitive, usually with in, into, or through: will it fit in the trunk? (помещаться, влезать, входить)
examples: Six people fit in that car if nobody has luggage.
The couch had fit through the door on the way in, somehow.

senses.head: Install, equip with
body: Regular in American English — fitted, not invariant fit: the room was fitted with sprinklers. British English prefers fitted for every sense. (устанавливать, оборудовать, оснащать)
examples: They fitted the whole floor with new smoke alarms.
The van has been fitted with a lift.

senses.head: Tailor or measure someone
body: Also regular: the tailor fitted the jacket, the optician fitted her for lenses. The person, not the garment, is often the object. (подгонять по фигуре, снимать мерку)
examples: The tailor fitted the jacket in twenty minutes.
She has been fitted for a brace twice this year.

senses.head: Fit in — belong among people
body: Of a person among people: he never fit in at that school. American English allows the invariant fit here; fitted in sounds British. (вписываться, приживаться, ладить)
examples: He never fit in at that school.
New hires fit in faster when someone shows them around.

senses.head: Fit someone in (schedule)
body: Of appointments and errands squeezed into a full day: can the doctor fit me in Thursday? (втиснуть, найти время для)
examples: The dentist fit me in at four.
She has fit two more meetings into an already full day.

entries.forms: fit /fɪt/ · fit /fɪt/ or fitted /ˈfɪtɪd/ · fit /fɪt/ or fitted /ˈfɪtɪd/
entries.register: everyday — clothes fit, stories fit the facts, people fit in
entries.pattern: no change in the "right size" sense
entries.contrast: American English splits the two senses. "Be the right size" keeps the invariant fit: the jacket fit me perfectly last year. "Install, tailor, or adjust" is regular: the optician fitted her for new lenses, the room was fitted with sprinklers. British English prefers fitted for both.
entries.verb type: stative in the core senses — being the right size or suiting something is a property, not an act, and it resists the progressive: ✗ these jeans are fitting me. The install and tailor senses (fitted the room with sprinklers) are ordinary action verbs.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the key fit the lock and the tailor fitted the jacket, intransitive with a place phrase (six people fit in that car, he never fit in at that school).
entries.passive: no in the stative senses — ✗ the lock was fit by the key, ✗ I am not fit by anything in that closet. Yes in the dynamic ones: the van has been fitted with a lift, she has been fitted for a brace twice this year.
entries.phrasal verbs: fit in · fit in with · fit out · fit up

entries.meaning: To say what is likely to happen, especially with weather, money, or demand.
examples: The service forecasts snow above five thousand feet.
Rain was forecast for Thursday afternoon.
The bureau had forecast clear skies for the whole weekend.
We forecast demand from three years of sales data.
Analysts forecast a slowdown months before it arrived.
Nobody has forecast a swing this large.
The early strikes forecast a long and bitter winter.
Nothing in the data had forecast the collapse.

senses.head: Predict the weather
body: The everyday sense, and usually passive when the forecaster is not named: rain is forecast for Thursday. (предсказывать (погоду), давать прогноз)
examples: The service forecasts snow above five thousand feet.
Rain was forecast for Thursday afternoon.
The bureau had forecast clear skies for the whole weekend.

senses.head: Project a business figure
body: Finance and planning: analysts forecast growth, companies forecast demand. Forecasted turns up here and is not flatly wrong, but forecast is safer in edited prose. (прогнозировать, планировать (показатели))
examples: We forecast demand from three years of sales data.
Analysts forecast a slowdown months before it arrived.
Nobody has forecast a swing this large.

senses.head: Foretell, foreshadow
body: A non-technical, slightly formal use in which an event itself forecasts what follows. Less common than foreshadow. (предвещать, предрекать)
examples: The early strikes forecast a long and bitter winter.
Nothing in the data had forecast the collapse.

entries.register: everyday — weather and business talk both use it without a second thought
entries.contrast: Forecast is the form to use in all three slots — rain was forecast for Tuesday. Forecasted appears in weather and finance writing and is not flatly wrong, but forecast is the safer choice in edited prose. Follows cast.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 3 (the early strikes forecast a long winter) shades toward the stative 'foreshadow', where an event simply points to what follows.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the prediction, a noun phrase or a that-clause (analysts forecast a slowdown, the service forecasts snow above five thousand feet).
entries.passive: yes, and it is the default when no forecaster is named — rain was forecast for Thursday afternoon.

entries.meaning: To strike something, to reach a level or a place, or to arrive somewhere suddenly and do damage.
examples: Don't hit your brother.
He hit the ball over the fence in the second inning.
The car has hit that same post twice.
A truck hit the guardrail and rolled.
Two deer have been hit on that stretch this month.
Gas prices have hit five dollars a gallon.
The thermometer hit a hundred and four on Sunday.
Storms hit that coast every fall.
The news had hit the wires before the family was told.
Let's hit the road before the traffic starts.
We hit three record stores in one afternoon.
It hit me halfway home that I had left my laptop there.
The full cost has not hit him yet.
She hit on a way to cut the wiring in half.
Somebody had hit on the same solution two years earlier.
They hit it off at the wedding and married a year later.
The two departments have never hit it off.
Hit me up when you get in.
He has hit every friend he has up for money.
She hit the brakes and we all lurched forward.
My father hit the roof when he saw the bill.

senses.head: Strike with force
body: The core sense, with a hand or an object: hit someone, hit the ball, hit the wall. Never hitted. (ударять, бить)
examples: Don't hit your brother.
He hit the ball over the fence in the second inning.
The car has hit that same post twice.

senses.head: Collide with, crash into
body: Of vehicles and moving things. The victim usually appears in the passive — she was hit by a car. (врезаться, наезжать, сбивать)
examples: A truck hit the guardrail and rolled.
Two deer have been hit on that stretch this month.

senses.head: Reach a level or number
body: Prices, temperatures, populations, and milestones all hit figures. Very common in news writing. (достигать (уровня), доходить до)
examples: Gas prices have hit five dollars a gallon.
The thermometer hit a hundred and four on Sunday.

senses.head: Strike an area or group
body: Of something that arrives suddenly and does damage: a storm, a recession, a scandal. (обрушиваться, поражать, ударять по)
examples: Storms hit that coast every fall.
The news had hit the wires before the family was told.

senses.head: Go to a place
body: Casual American usage: hit the gym, hit the store, and hit the road, meaning leave. (отправиться куда-л., заглянуть, махнуть)
examples: Let's hit the road before the traffic starts.
We hit three record stores in one afternoon.

senses.head: Occur to someone
body: Of a realization arriving all at once. The thought is the subject and the person is the object: it hit me that... (осенить, дойти (до сознания))
examples: It hit me halfway home that I had left my laptop there.
The full cost has not hit him yet.

senses.head: Hit on — flirt; devise
body: Hit on an idea is to think of it; hit on someone is to make a pass at them. Same words, very different registers, and only context separates them. (натолкнуться на (мысль); клеиться, приставать)
examples: She hit on a way to cut the wiring in half.
Somebody had hit on the same solution two years earlier.

senses.head: Hit it off — click
body: Fixed phrase, always with it, and almost always about a first meeting. (сразу поладить, найти общий язык)
examples: They hit it off at the wedding and married a year later.
The two departments have never hit it off.

senses.head: Hit up — contact, ask
body: Informal and recent: hit me up when you land, he hit his brother up for a loan. (обратиться к, стрельнуть (что-л. у кого-л.))
examples: Hit me up when you get in.
He has hit every friend he has up for money.

senses.head: Hit the brakes, the roof
body: A family of fixed phrases where hit means start or go to. Hit the roof and hit the ceiling both mean lose your temper; hit the sack means go to bed. (ударить по тормозам; сесть за учёбу; взорваться от злости)
examples: She hit the brakes and we all lurched forward.
My father hit the roof when he saw the bill.

entries.register: everyday — one of the busiest verbs in American speech, with a dozen live idioms
entries.contrast: Never hitted. Because all three forms are hit, the auxiliary is the only signal: ✗ I have hitted it — write I hit it yesterday for the finished past and I have hit it twice for the participle. The compound uppercut and the near-synonym cut behave the same way.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and sudden; a large family of fixed idioms (hit the road, hit it off, hit the roof) rides on the same verb.
entries.transitivity: transitive in nearly every sense, with the object obligatory (hit the ball, gas prices have hit five dollars); intransitive only inside phrasal frames like hit back and hit out.
entries.passive: yes — she was hit by a car, two deer have been hit on that stretch this month. The idioms refuse it: ✗ it off was hit by them at the wedding.
entries.phrasal verbs: hit back · hit it off · hit on · hit out · hit up

entries.meaning: To raise something heavy, usually with ropes, a crane, or a lot of effort.
examples: Two crew members hoist the mainsail every morning.
They hoisted the piano through a third-floor window.
By noon they had hoisted every crate onto the deck.
She hoists her daughter onto her shoulders to see the parade.
He hoisted the duffel bag into the overhead bin.
They hoist the flag at sunrise and lower it at sunset.
The banner has been hoisted over the entrance since Friday.
He was hoist with his own petard when the memo leaked.
The senator has been hoist with his own petard more than once.

senses.head: Raise with rope or crane
body: The main sense, and regular in modern American English — they hoisted the piano through the window. The invariant hoist is an older participle. (поднимать (лебёдкой, тросом), водружать)
examples: Two crew members hoist the mainsail every morning.
They hoisted the piano through a third-floor window.
By noon they had hoisted every crate onto the deck.

senses.head: Lift up bodily
body: Everyday use for lifting something or someone with no machinery involved. (вскидывать, подхватывать (на руки, на плечи))
examples: She hoists her daughter onto her shoulders to see the parade.
He hoisted the duffel bag into the overhead bin.

senses.head: Raise a flag or banner
body: Ceremonial and nautical: hoist the colors, hoist the flag. Usually passive when the thing stays up. (поднимать (флаг), вывешивать)
examples: They hoist the flag at sunrise and lower it at sunset.
The banner has been hoisted over the entrance since Friday.

senses.head: Hoist with one's own petard
body: The one place the invariant hoist survives — from Hamlet, meaning blown up by your own bomb. A fixed phrase; do not rebuild it with other words. (попасть в собственную ловушку, угодить в свои же сети)
examples: He was hoist with his own petard when the memo leaked.
The senator has been hoist with his own petard more than once.

entries.forms: hoist /hɔɪst/ · hoist /hɔɪst/ or hoisted /ˈhɔɪstɪd/ · hoist /hɔɪst/ or hoisted /ˈhɔɪstɪd/
entries.register: neutral — ordinary in writing and on a job site, less common in casual speech
entries.contrast: In ordinary modern American English this verb is regular: they hoisted the flag. The invariant hoist is an older participle that survives mainly in one idiom — hoist with his own petard, blown up by his own bomb. Write hoisted unless you are quoting the idiom.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the invariant participle survives only in the frozen hoist with his own petard.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the heavy thing raised (they hoisted the piano through a third-floor window), and it is obligatory.
entries.passive: yes — the banner has been hoisted over the entrance since Friday, and the idiom is passive by definition: he was hoist with his own petard.

entries.meaning: To cause pain or damage, or to feel pain.
examples: My shoulder hurts when it rains.
My knee hurt all week after the hike.
That tooth has hurt on and off since Christmas.
I hurt my back moving the couch on Saturday.
Nobody has been hurt at that intersection this year.
It hurt to hear her say that.
He never meant to hurt anyone.
The scandal had hurt the company long before the lawsuit.
Skipping practice hurts the whole team.
It wouldn't hurt to call ahead and check.
A second opinion never hurt anybody.
Small farms are hurting after two dry summers.
He was hurting for cash until the check cleared.

senses.head: Feel pain
body: Intransitive, with the body part as subject: my knee hurts. There is no hurted, so the time word decides whether it is now or over. (болеть (о части тела))
examples: My shoulder hurts when it rains.
My knee hurt all week after the hike.
That tooth has hurt on and off since Christmas.

senses.head: Injure, cause physical pain
body: Transitive and often reflexive: I hurt my back. The passive participle doubles as an adjective — three people were hurt means injured rather than forming a true passive. (ушибить, повредить, причинить боль)
examples: I hurt my back moving the couch on Saturday.
Nobody has been hurt at that intersection this year.

senses.head: Wound someone's feelings
body: With a person or feelings as object. One of the commonest uses of the verb in ordinary speech. (обижать, задевать, ранить)
examples: It hurt to hear her say that.
He never meant to hurt anyone.

senses.head: Damage, harm something
body: Of reputations, chances, sales, and teams — the object is a thing rather than a body. (вредить, наносить ущерб)
examples: The scandal had hurt the company long before the lawsuit.
Skipping practice hurts the whole team.

senses.head: It wouldn't hurt to
body: A fixed negative frame for giving advice gently, and its cousin it never hurt anyone. (не помешало бы, не мешает)
examples: It wouldn't hurt to call ahead and check.
A second opinion never hurt anybody.

senses.head: Be hurting — be struggling
body: Informal and progressive only: an industry, a town, or a person short of money is hurting. (бедствовать, туго приходиться)
examples: Small farms are hurting after two dry summers.
He was hurting for cash until the check cleared.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: No hurted. Since the past is spelled and said exactly like the present, the time word decides: my knee hurts is now, my knee hurt all week is over. The participle doubles as an adjective — three people were hurt — where it means "injured" rather than forming a true passive.
entries.verb type: both — action in I hurt my back and the scandal hurt the company, but the intransitive my knee hurts names a state (it still takes the progressive: my knee is hurting). Be hurting for money is progressive-only.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with the body part as subject (my shoulder hurts when it rains), transitive with a person, a feeling, or a thing as object (it hurt her, skipping practice hurts the whole team).
entries.passive: restricted — nobody has been hurt at that intersection is standard, but the participle there is closer to the adjective injured than to a true passive, and the intransitive my knee hurts has no passive at all.

entries.meaning: To enter data into a computer or a system.
examples: Please input the account number before you hit save.
She input all four hundred records by hand last week.
Someone has input the wrong shipping address.
The clerk had input the figures twice by mistake.
The sensor inputs a fresh reading every second.
Whatever you input, the model rounds it to two decimals.

senses.head: Enter data
body: The main sense. Inputted is widespread in computing and business writing, but input is what dictionaries list first, and entered or typed in usually reads better than either. (вводить (данные), заносить)
examples: Please input the account number before you hit save.
She input all four hundred records by hand last week.
Someone has input the wrong shipping address.
The clerk had input the figures twice by mistake.

senses.head: Feed into a process
body: Engineering and modeling use: values, energy, or materials input to a system. The noun is usually the better choice — the inputs to the model. (подавать на вход, вводить (в систему))
examples: The sensor inputs a fresh reading every second.
Whatever you input, the model rounds it to two decimals.

entries.register: neutral — computing and business writing; speech prefers enter or type in
entries.contrast: Inputted is widespread in computing and business writing, but input is the form dictionaries list first and the safer one in edited prose. Note also that the noun input (we need your input) is much commoner than the verb — entered or typed in usually reads better than either. The vowel is the one in foot, as in put.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the noun input is far commoner than the verb, which stays in computing and business writing.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the data (input the account number before you hit save), and it is obligatory.
entries.passive: yes — the wrong shipping address has been input — though entered or typed in usually reads better in the same slot.

entries.meaning: To set one thing inside another — a small map on a large one, a panel in a door.
examples: The builder inset the shelves into the wall when he remodeled the kitchen.
The jeweler had inset three small stones along the band.
Cartographers often inset a detail map in the lower corner.
This template insets the caption automatically.
A photograph of the author has been inset on the back cover.

senses.head: Place within a recess
body: Building and craft work: shelves inset into a wall, stones inset in a ring. The participle is what you usually meet — an inset panel. (вставлять, врезать, утапливать)
examples: The builder inset the shelves into the wall when he remodeled the kitchen.
The jeweler had inset three small stones along the band.

senses.head: Inset a map or picture
body: Cartography and publishing. The noun — the small map in the corner — is stressed IN-set, while many speakers move the verb's stress to in-SET. (помещать врезку (карту, иллюстрацию))
examples: Cartographers often inset a detail map in the lower corner.
This template insets the caption automatically.
A photograph of the author has been inset on the back cover.

entries.register: rare — building, jewelry, and publishing shop talk, usually met as an inset panel
entries.contrast: The noun — a small map or picture inside a larger one — is stressed IN-set; as a verb many speakers move the stress to the second syllable, in-SET. Forms follow set, and the participle is the one you usually see: an inset panel.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; in practice the participle does most of the work as an adjective (an inset panel).
entries.transitivity: transitive, normally with a place phrase — inset the shelves into the wall, inset a detail map in the lower corner.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the usual form — a photograph of the author has been inset on the back cover.

entries.meaning: To alternate shots from two different scenes in a film or video.
examples: Editors often intercut an interview with archive footage.
She intercut the wedding scene with shots of the empty church.
In the 1962 version the editor intercut the trial with the riot outside.
The trailer has been intercut with clips from the sequel.
The memoir intercuts the trial with scenes from her childhood.
He had intercut the two timelines so tightly that viewers lost track.

senses.head: Alternate two scenes in editing
body: Film and video vocabulary, very close to crosscut. The frame is intercut A with B or intercut between two things. (чередовать кадры, монтировать параллельно)
examples: Editors often intercut an interview with archive footage.
She intercut the wedding scene with shots of the empty church.
In the 1962 version the editor intercut the trial with the riot outside.
The trailer has been intercut with clips from the sequel.

senses.head: Interleave, break up with
body: Extended from the film sense to writing and performance — a narrative intercut with letters, a lecture intercut with jokes. (перемежать, прерывать (чем-л.))
examples: The memoir intercuts the trial with scenes from her childhood.
He had intercut the two timelines so tightly that viewers lost track.

entries.register: rare — film and video editing vocabulary, seldom used outside it
entries.contrast: Film vocabulary, very close to crosscut: to intercut is to alternate two lines of action in the editing. Forms come from cut.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; film and video editing vocabulary, extended to writing and performance.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the frame is intercut A with B or intercut between two lines of action (she intercut the wedding scene with shots of the empty church).
entries.passive: yes — the trailer has been intercut with clips from the sequel.

entries.meaning: To make cloth by looping yarn with needles, or, figuratively, to join and grow together.
examples: She knits a sweater every winter.
They knitted hats for the shelter all last November.
He has knitted three blankets since he retired.
The fracture knit faster than the doctor expected.
The bone has knit cleanly, so the cast comes off Friday.
She knits her brows whenever the subject of money comes up.
He had knit his brows before I finished the question.
Grief has knit that family closer than anything else could.
It takes years to knit a group of strangers into a crew.
The new rail line knit the two towns into one labor market.
She had knit the interviews together into a single narrative.

senses.head: Knit with yarn and needles
body: The literal craft sense, and the one American English makes regular — she knitted a scarf. The k is silent. (вязать (спицами))
examples: She knits a sweater every winter.
They knitted hats for the shelter all last November.
He has knitted three blankets since he retired.

senses.head: Of bone: heal together
body: Medical and everyday alike: a fracture knits. This sense keeps the invariant knit. (срастаться (о кости))
examples: The fracture knit faster than the doctor expected.
The bone has knit cleanly, so the cast comes off Friday.

senses.head: Knit one's brows
body: A fixed phrase for frowning in thought or worry. Invariant knit, and rather literary. (хмурить брови, нахмуриться)
examples: She knits her brows whenever the subject of money comes up.
He had knit his brows before I finished the question.

senses.head: Bind people closely together
body: Figurative, and usually passive or adjectival — a tightly knit family, a close-knit town. Invariant knit. (сплачивать, объединять)
examples: Grief has knit that family closer than anything else could.
It takes years to knit a group of strangers into a crew.

senses.head: Join parts into a whole
body: Of arguments, regions, or organizations drawn together into one thing. Formal, and often knit together. (соединять, связывать воедино)
examples: The new rail line knit the two towns into one labor market.
She had knit the interviews together into a single narrative.

entries.forms: knit /nɪt/ · knit /nɪt/ or knitted /ˈnɪtɪd/ · knit /nɪt/ or knitted /ˈnɪtɪd/
entries.register: everyday — ordinary for yarn, for a healing bone, and for a close-knit family
entries.pattern: no change in the figurative sense
entries.contrast: The k is silent. American English uses regular knitted for yarn and needles — she knitted a scarf — and keeps invariant knit for the figurative senses: the bone knit cleanly, a tightly knit family, he knit his brows. Both are standard; the meaning picks the form.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense; the participle is adjectival in a tightly knit family and a close-knit town.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with yarn, brows, or people (she knitted a scarf, he knit his brows), intransitive of a healing bone (the fracture knit faster than the doctor expected).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the interviews had been knit together into a single narrative. The bone sense is intransitive and has none: ✗ the bone was knit cleanly by itself.

entries.meaning: To allow something to happen, and, in a long list of fixed phrases, to release, admit, disappoint, or stop.
examples: My parents never let me stay out past ten.
He lets the dog sleep on the couch.
They have let the lease run out.
Let me know when the package arrives.
Let's take the back road.
Let go of the rope on three.
The company has let forty people go since January.
Somebody let the dog out during the night.
She had let him in through the back before anyone saw.
He let the whole crew down and knew it.
The team has never let its fans down at home.
The judge let him off with a fine.
Somebody had let off a firecracker in the hallway.
The rain let up around four.
The pressure on the department has not let up all year.
She never let on that she had already read it.
He has not let on how much the repair cost.
I can't afford the rent, let alone a car payment.
Let him alone until he's finished.
I let it slide the first two times.
He had let slip the date before the announcement.
They let the upstairs flat to a student last autumn.
The cottage has been let every summer since 1990.

senses.head: Allow, permit
body: The core sense, with a bare infinitive after the object: let me go, never ✗ let me to go. Never letted, and do not confuse it with leave. (позволять, разрешать, давать)
examples: My parents never let me stay out past ten.
He lets the dog sleep on the couch.
They have let the lease run out.

senses.head: Let me, let's — propose
body: Let me offers to do something; let's, a contraction of let us, proposes doing it together. The standard negative is let's not. (давай(те), позволь(те))
examples: Let me know when the package arrives.
Let's take the back road.

senses.head: Let go — release; fire
body: Literally releasing your grip, figuratively giving up on something, and — as let someone go — the polite office word for firing them. (отпускать, выпускать из рук; увольнять)
examples: Let go of the rope on three.
The company has let forty people go since January.

senses.head: Let in, let out
body: Of doors, animals, and people. Let out also means end, for classes and shows — school lets out at three. (впускать; выпускать)
examples: Somebody let the dog out during the night.
She had let him in through the back before anyone saw.

senses.head: Let down — disappoint
body: Let someone down is to fail them; literally, let down a hem or a rope is to lower it. The noun letdown comes from the first. (подводить, разочаровывать)
examples: He let the whole crew down and knew it.
The team has never let its fans down at home.

senses.head: Let off — excuse; set off
body: Let someone off is to spare them punishment, let off steam is to vent, and let off fireworks is to set them off. (отпустить, простить; выпустить (пар), запустить (фейерверк))
examples: The judge let him off with a fine.
Somebody had let off a firecracker in the hallway.

senses.head: Let up — ease off, stop
body: Intransitive, of rain, pressure, pain, or effort: the rain never let up. (утихать, ослабевать, прекращаться)
examples: The rain let up around four.
The pressure on the department has not let up all year.

senses.head: Let on — reveal, admit
body: Informal, and usually negative: don't let on that you know. (выдавать (тайну), подавать вид)
examples: She never let on that she had already read it.
He has not let on how much the repair cost.

senses.head: Let alone — much less
body: A fixed connector following a negative: he can't walk, let alone run. Separately, let someone alone means leave them in peace. (не говоря уже о)
examples: I can't afford the rent, let alone a car payment.
Let him alone until he's finished.

senses.head: Let it slide or slip
body: Let it slide is to overlook something, let it slip is to reveal it by accident, and let it drop is to stop discussing it. (спускать на тормозах; проговориться; замять)
examples: I let it slide the first two times.
He had let slip the date before the announcement.

senses.head: Rent out (British)
body: British English for renting property out — rooms to let. American English says rent, though sublet is standard on both sides and comes from this sense. (сдавать внаём)
examples: They let the upstairs flat to a student last autumn.
The cottage has been let every summer since 1990.

entries.register: everyday — a core verb of permission and of a dozen phrasal verbs
entries.contrast: Never letted. Two things to keep apart: let (allow) and leave (go away from) — ✗ Let me alone at the station — and let the verb versus let's, a contraction of let us. British English also uses let for "rent out," which is where sublet comes from.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and causative, taking a bare infinitive after its object (let me go, never ✗ let me to go); let's is a frozen first-person imperative formula.
entries.transitivity: transitive — object plus a bare infinitive or a particle (let the dog out, let forty people go); the object is obligatory: ✗ he lets.
entries.passive: restricted — the causative has no ordinary passive (✗ he was let stay out past ten; say was allowed to stay), but the fixed phrasal and rental uses do passivize: forty people were let go, the cottage has been let every summer since 1990.
entries.phrasal verbs: let down · let in · let in on · let off · let on · let out · let up

entries.meaning: To give an actor a part that does not suit them, or to put a person or an issue in the wrong role.
examples: Directors miscast comic actors in serious parts all the time.
The studio miscast the lead and the film never recovered.
She has been miscast in every romantic comedy she has made.
Making a shy manager the spokesman miscasts him completely.
He had miscast himself as a peacemaker and everyone knew it.
The bill has been miscast as a tax increase.
Critics miscast the study as proof of something it never claimed.

senses.head: Miscast an actor
body: Nearly always passive — he was badly miscast as the villain. Forms come from cast; miscasted is not standard. (неправильно распределить роли, ошибиться с актёром)
examples: Directors miscast comic actors in serious parts all the time.
The studio miscast the lead and the film never recovered.
She has been miscast in every romantic comedy she has made.

senses.head: Put in the wrong role
body: The figurative use outside the theater: giving a person a job or a public part that does not fit them. (поставить не на своё место)
examples: Making a shy manager the spokesman miscasts him completely.
He had miscast himself as a peacemaker and everyone knew it.

senses.head: Frame an issue wrongly
body: Journalistic, close to mischaracterize: presenting something as the wrong kind of problem. (представлять в ложном свете, искажать суть)
examples: The bill has been miscast as a tax increase.
Critics miscast the study as proof of something it never claimed.

entries.register: rare — entertainment criticism, nearly always passive, and prefixed from cast
entries.contrast: Nearly always passive — he was badly miscast as the villain. Forms come from cast; miscasted is not standard.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and met almost entirely as a passive participle.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the actor, the person, or the issue (the studio miscast the lead, critics miscast the study).
entries.passive: yes, and it is the normal form — he was badly miscast as the villain, the bill has been miscast as a tax increase.

entries.meaning: To read something wrong, or to misjudge a person or a situation. The past and participle keep the spelling but are said mis-RED.
examples: I misread the departure time and missed the flight.
She misreads my handwriting every single time.
He had misread the label and used the wrong solvent.
People often misread politeness as agreement.
The market has misread the Fed twice this year.
The pilot misread the altimeter in the fog.
It is easy to misread a scale marked that finely.

senses.head: Read words incorrectly
body: The literal sense — wrong time, wrong number, wrong word. Nothing on the page separates past from present; only the vowel does. (прочитать неправильно, ошибиться при чтении)
examples: I misread the departure time and missed the flight.
She misreads my handwriting every single time.
He had misread the label and used the wrong solvent.

senses.head: Misjudge a person or situation
body: The commoner figurative sense: reading a mood, a market, or an intention wrong. (неверно истолковать, неправильно понять)
examples: People often misread politeness as agreement.
The market has misread the Fed twice this year.

senses.head: Misread an instrument or signal
body: Technical: taking the wrong value off a gauge, a chart, or a test. Often the named cause in an incident report. (неверно снять показания)
examples: The pilot misread the altimeter in the fog.
It is easy to misread a scale marked that finely.

entries.register: everyday — I misread the schedule is ordinary American speech
entries.third person: misreads /ˌmɪsˈridz/ · -ing form: misreading /ˌmɪsˈridɪŋ/ (both keep the REED vowel)
entries.contrast: The same trap as read: the spelling never moves, but the past and participle rhyme with bed. I misread the schedule is past if you say mis-RED and present if you say mis-REED — nothing on the page tells you which.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both the literal and the figurative sense.
entries.transitivity: transitive — object obligatory in practice (misread the label, misread the market, misread politeness as agreement).
entries.passive: yes — the altimeter had been misread in the fog — though the active, with the person who erred as subject, is far commoner.

entries.meaning: To balance one thing against another so that the two effects cancel out.
examples: A federal credit offsets part of the cost.
Higher fuel prices offset most of the savings last quarter.
Rising rents have offset every raise she has gotten.
You can offset capital losses against gains in the same year.
The refund had offset most of what she owed.
The airline says it offsets every flight it sells.
The company has offset less than a tenth of what it emits.
Offset the second row of tiles by half a width.
The builder had offset the chimney a foot from center.

senses.head: Balance out, compensate for
body: The everyday sense: a gain that cancels a loss. Forms follow set, so never offsetted. (компенсировать, возмещать, уравновешивать)
examples: A federal credit offsets part of the cost.
Higher fuel prices offset most of the savings last quarter.
Rising rents have offset every raise she has gotten.

senses.head: Set one amount against another
body: Bookkeeping and tax: offset losses against gains, offset a debt. The noun offset names the entry itself. (зачитывать, засчитывать (в счёт другого))
examples: You can offset capital losses against gains in the same year.
The refund had offset most of what she owed.

senses.head: Offset emissions
body: Climate and corporate usage: paying for reductions elsewhere to cancel your own emissions. Almost always with carbon or emissions. (компенсировать выбросы)
examples: The airline says it offsets every flight it sells.
The company has offset less than a tenth of what it emits.

senses.head: Place at a distance from
body: Technical, in building, design, and typography: one element set off to the side of another. The participle-adjective is common — an offset hinge. (смещать, сдвигать (относительно чего-л.))
examples: Offset the second row of tiles by half a width.
The builder had offset the chimney a foot from center.

entries.register: neutral — ordinary in business, tax, and climate writing, less common in speech
entries.contrast: The noun and adjective are stressed AWF-set; as a verb many speakers move the stress to the second syllable, awf-SET. Forms follow set — no offsetted.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, though a federal credit offsets part of the cost states a standing relationship as much as an event.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is what gets balanced out (offset capital losses against gains, the airline offsets every flight it sells).
entries.passive: yes — most of the savings were offset by higher fuel prices, the chimney had been offset a foot from center.

entries.meaning: To produce something, especially data sent out by a machine or a program.
examples: The script outputs a CSV file to the same folder.
Set the flag if you want the tool to output JSON instead.
The model has output the same error twice.
The old printer output three blank pages before it jammed.
By Friday the plant had output more units than in the whole prior month.

senses.head: Produce data or a file
body: Computing use: a program outputs a file, a value, or an error. Outputted is common in programming writing, but keep output in edited prose. (выводить (данные), выдавать)
examples: The script outputs a CSV file to the same folder.
Set the flag if you want the tool to output JSON instead.
The model has output the same error twice.

senses.head: Produce a quantity of goods
body: Industry and economics: a plant, a mine, or a writer outputs a measurable amount. The noun is far commoner than the verb here. (производить, выпускать (продукцию))
examples: The old printer output three blank pages before it jammed.
By Friday the plant had output more units than in the whole prior month.

entries.register: neutral — computing and economics writing; in speech the noun does the work
entries.contrast: Like input, the noun is much commoner than the verb, and outputted shows up in programming writing. Keep output in all three slots in edited prose. The Russian gloss here is the spreadsheet's; in practice the verb means "produce" or "send data out," not "go out."
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; like input, the noun is much commoner than the verb, and the verb means 'produce' or 'send out', not 'go out'.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is what the machine or plant produces (the script outputs a CSV file to the same folder).
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical but clumsy (the same error has been output twice); careful writing reaches for produced, written, or returned instead.

entries.meaning: To stay somewhere longer than you were welcome or allowed to.
examples: Guests who overstay their welcome rarely notice it.
Nobody wants to overstay at a party that has clearly ended.
We have overstayed our welcome — let's go.
He overstayed his visa by three months.
By August she had overstayed the ninety days her permit allowed.

senses.head: Overstay one's welcome
body: The commonest use, and nearly always with welcome as the object. Regular in real American English — write overstayed. (загоститься, засидеться в гостях)
examples: Guests who overstay their welcome rarely notice it.
Nobody wants to overstay at a party that has clearly ended.
We have overstayed our welcome — let's go.

senses.head: Stay past a legal limit
body: Immigration and parking: overstay a visa, overstay the meter. Always regular in this sense. (просрочить (визу, срок пребывания))
examples: He overstayed his visa by three months.
By August she had overstayed the ninety days her permit allowed.

entries.forms: overstay /ˌoʊvərˈsteɪ/ · overstay /ˌoʊvərˈsteɪ/ or overstayed /ˌoʊvərˈsteɪd/ · overstay /ˌoʊvərˈsteɪ/ or overstayed /ˌoʊvərˈsteɪd/
entries.register: everyday — familiar to everyone through overstay your welcome and visa talk
entries.contrast: In real American English this verb is regular: he overstayed his visa, we have overstayed our welcome. The invariant listing comes from the source spreadsheet; overstayed is what you should write. It sits in this group for completeness, not as a model.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and a regular verb (overstayed) in real American English despite the invariant listing.
