entries.transitivity: both — normally transitive with a fixed object (overstay your welcome, overstay a visa), intransitive of lingering (nobody wants to overstay at a party that has clearly ended).
entries.passive: no in real use — the object is a possessed noun, which blocks it: ✗ his welcome was overstayed, ✗ the visa was overstayed by him.

entries.meaning: To read a text closely to catch mistakes before it is published. The past and participle keep the spelling but are said PROOF-red.
examples: She proofreads every contract before it goes out.
Would you proofread this paragraph for me?
I proofread the newsletter twice last night and still missed a typo.
The manuscript has been proofread by two editors.
He had proofread only half the galleys when the deadline passed.
Every page has been proofread against the marked-up copy.

senses.head: Check a text for errors
body: The everyday sense — a last pass for typos, spelling, and punctuation rather than for content. (вычитывать, корректировать текст)
examples: She proofreads every contract before it goes out.
Would you proofread this paragraph for me?
I proofread the newsletter twice last night and still missed a typo.
The manuscript has been proofread by two editors.

senses.head: Read proofs against the copy
body: The strict trade sense: comparing typeset proofs word by word against the edited manuscript. A proofreader does this; an editor does something else. (сверять корректуру с оригиналом)
examples: He had proofread only half the galleys when the deadline passed.
Every page has been proofread against the marked-up copy.

entries.register: everyday — anyone who writes at work uses it
entries.third person: proofreads /ˈprufˌridz/ · -ing form: proofreading /ˈprufˌridɪŋ/ (both keep the REED vowel)
entries.contrast: The same pronunciation trap as read. I proofread it last night is PROOF-red; I proofread everything twice is PROOF-reed. Nothing in the spelling separates them.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; one careful pass over a text rather than a state.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the text as object (would you proofread this paragraph?), intransitive of the job itself (she proofreads for a living).
entries.passive: yes — the manuscript has been proofread by two editors, every page has been proofread against the marked-up copy.

entries.meaning: To move something into a place or a position, and, by extension, to express, assign, or apply something.
examples: Put the milk back in the refrigerator.
I put the keys on the counter an hour ago.
Someone has put my chair out in the hallway.
Put it in your own words and it will make more sense.
She had put the objection more politely than I would have.
Investigators put the damage at two million dollars.
Nobody has put a firm date on the opening yet.
They put forty thousand dollars into the renovation.
He has put years into that manuscript.
The chair put the motion to a vote.
The proposal had been put to the board twice already.
Put on a jacket — it's colder than it looks.
The school has put on the same play three years running.
We put the trip off until spring.
The smell had put half the class off lunch.
I have put up with that noise for two years.
She put up with a lot before she quit.
Crews put the fire out before it reached the barn.
The company has put out three statements in two days.
Put your name down on the list by the door.
They had to put the old dog down last spring.
They put up a new warehouse on the lot last year.
My aunt has put us up every summer since I was small.
Put me through to the front desk, please.
She has put two kids through college on one salary.

senses.head: Place something somewhere
body: The core sense, and it needs a place: put the milk in the fridge, not ✗ put the milk. Never putted — that belongs to golf's putt. (класть, ставить, помещать)
examples: Put the milk back in the refrigerator.
I put the keys on the counter an hour ago.
Someone has put my chair out in the hallway.

senses.head: Express in words
body: Almost always with an adverb or a manner phrase: to put it bluntly, how would you put it?, well put. (выражать, формулировать, сказать)
examples: Put it in your own words and it will make more sense.
She had put the objection more politely than I would have.

senses.head: Assign a figure or blame
body: The frame is put X at a number or put X on a person: put the damage at two million, put the blame on the contractor. (оценивать (в), относить, возлагать (вину))
examples: Investigators put the damage at two million dollars.
Nobody has put a firm date on the opening yet.

senses.head: Put money or effort into
body: Put money into a business, put work into a project, put your heart into something. (вкладывать (деньги, силы, труд))
examples: They put forty thousand dollars into the renovation.
He has put years into that manuscript.

senses.head: Put a question to someone
body: Formal: put the motion to a vote, put the question to the committee. Courtroom and debate talk adds I put it to you that... (поставить (вопрос), вынести (на рассмотрение))
examples: The chair put the motion to a vote.
The proposal had been put to the board twice already.

senses.head: Put on — wear, stage
body: Four unrelated uses of one phrase: put on a coat, put on ten pounds, put on a play, and put on an act. You're putting me on means you're kidding me. (надевать; набирать (вес); ставить (спектакль); притворяться)
examples: Put on a jacket — it's colder than it looks.
The school has put on the same play three years running.

senses.head: Put off — postpone; repel
body: Put off a meeting is to postpone it; something that puts you off disgusts or discourages you. The adjective off-putting comes from the second. (откладывать; отталкивать, отбивать охоту)
examples: We put the trip off until spring.
The smell had put half the class off lunch.

senses.head: Put up with — tolerate
body: A fixed three-word phrasal verb; the object always follows the whole thing — put up with the noise, never ✗ put the noise up with. (мириться с, терпеть)
examples: I have put up with that noise for two years.
She put up with a lot before she quit.

senses.head: Put out — extinguish; issue; inconvenience
body: Put out a fire, put out a statement, or put someone out, meaning trouble them. As an adjective, put out means annoyed. (тушить; выпускать, издавать; доставлять неудобство)
examples: Crews put the fire out before it reached the barn.
The company has put out three statements in two days.

senses.head: Put down — record, suppress
body: Four uses that share nothing but the words: put your name down, put down a rebellion, put a dog down, and put someone down, meaning insult them. (записывать; подавлять; усыплять (животное); принижать)
examples: Put your name down on the list by the door.
They had to put the old dog down last spring.

senses.head: Put up — build; raise; accommodate
body: Put up a building or a shelf, put up your hand, or put someone up for the night. Put up a fight means resist. (строить, возводить; поднимать; приютить)
examples: They put up a new warehouse on the lot last year.
My aunt has put us up every summer since I was small.

senses.head: Put through — connect, endure
body: Put a call through is to connect it; put someone through something is to make them go through it; put someone through school is to pay for it. (соединять (по телефону); заставить пройти через; оплачивать учёбу)
examples: Put me through to the front desk, please.
She has put two kids through college on one salary.

entries.register: everyday — one of the handful of verbs no English sentence gets far without
entries.contrast: Putted is a real word, but it belongs to a different verb — golf's putt /pʌt/: she putted from twelve feet. The verb put never takes -ed: ✗ I putted the keys on the table. And the vowel is the one in foot, not the one in cut, so putting /ˈpʊtɪŋ/ and putting /ˈpʌtɪŋ/ are two different words.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; it needs a place or manner complement as much as it needs an object.
entries.transitivity: transitive, and the object alone is not enough: ✗ put the milk — put the milk back in the refrigerator. In the three-word put up with, the object follows the whole phrase: ✗ put the noise up with.
entries.passive: yes — the proposal had been put to the board twice already, my chair has been put out in the hallway.
entries.phrasal verbs: put across · put aside · put away · put back · put by · put down · put down to · put forward · put in · put in for · put off · put on · put out · put through · put together · put up · put up with · put upon

entries.meaning: To stop doing something, to leave a job for good, or to close a program.
examples: I quit eating sugar in January and lasted about six days.
You should quit checking your phone every two minutes.
She has quit trying to explain it to him.
She quit her job the week after the merger.
Three people have quit since the new manager arrived.
He had quit the team long before the season ended.
Quit it — you're going to break something.
My mother told us to quit fighting in the back seat.
Quit the app and open it again.
I quit Photoshop last night and the file was still locked this morning.
The installer won't run until you have quit every open program.
The mower quit halfway through the yard.
My knees have quit on me since I turned fifty.

senses.head: Stop doing something
body: Takes an -ing form, never an infinitive: quit smoking, not ✗quit to smoke. American English keeps quit in all three slots; quitted sounds British and dated. (бросать, переставать)
examples: I quit eating sugar in January and lasted about six days.
You should quit checking your phone every two minutes.
She has quit trying to explain it to him.

senses.head: Leave a job, resign
body: The commonest sense in daily American speech. Quit on someone adds the sense of abandoning them. (увольняться, уходить (с работы))
examples: She quit her job the week after the merger.
Three people have quit since the new manager arrived.
He had quit the team long before the season ended.

senses.head: Quit it, quit that
body: A blunt spoken imperative, used to children or close friends. Rude from a stranger. (прекрати, хватит)
examples: Quit it — you're going to break something.
My mother told us to quit fighting in the back seat.

senses.head: Close a program
body: Computing. On a Mac, Quit shuts the whole application down, while close only closes one window. (закрывать программу, выходить из приложения)
examples: Quit the app and open it again.
I quit Photoshop last night and the file was still locked this morning.
The installer won't run until you have quit every open program.

senses.head: Stop working, give out
body: Informal, of engines, appliances, and body parts. Often quit on someone. (отказывать, глохнуть, ломаться)
examples: The mower quit halfway through the yard.
My knees have quit on me since I turned fifty.

entries.register: everyday — the ordinary American word for stopping or leaving a job
entries.contrast: American English uses quit for all three forms — she quit her job in June. Quitted exists in older and British writing but sounds wrong to American ears. The frame is quit doing something (quit smoking), never quit to do something.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; it takes an -ing complement, never an infinitive: ✗ quit to smoke.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a job, an activity, or a program (she quit her job, quit checking your phone), intransitive when what is given up is understood (three people have quit since the new manager arrived).
entries.passive: restricted — barely used: ✗ her job was quit the week after the merger. Even the computing sense prefers the app was closed to was quit.

entries.meaning: To take in written words, and by extension to interpret, to state, or to display information.
examples: I read (REED) two newspapers every morning.
She read (RED) the whole novel on the flight to Chicago.
He has read that book three times.
Would you read this paragraph back to me?
He read the kids a story every night that summer.
By the time we got there the clerk had read the whole list aloud.
A good pitcher reads the batter's stance.
She read the room and dropped the subject.
We have read the market wrong twice this year.
That line reads as sarcastic in print.
The apology read as insincere to everyone who saw it.
The sign reads 'No entry after six.'
The original draft read differently on that point.
The plaque had read 'Founded 1902' before someone repainted it.
The gauge reads forty pounds.
The thermometer read ninety-eight at noon.
Someone from the utility has read the meter already.
The drive reads discs but won't burn them.
The scanner read the barcode on the second try.
The program has read the whole file into memory.
I need to read up on the new tax rules.
She read up on the company the night before the interview.
He has read up on every treatment option there is.
Don't read too much into a one-word answer.
The press read a threat into a fairly bland statement.
She read law at Oxford in the eighties.
He has read classics for three years now.

senses.head: Take in written words
body: The core sense. The spelling never changes, but the past and participle are said /rɛd/, exactly like the color red. (читать)
examples: I read (REED) two newspapers every morning.
She read (RED) the whole novel on the flight to Chicago.
He has read that book three times.

senses.head: Read aloud to someone
body: Frames: read to someone, read someone something, read something back/out. (читать вслух, зачитывать)
examples: Would you read this paragraph back to me?
He read the kids a story every night that summer.
By the time we got there the clerk had read the whole list aloud.

senses.head: Interpret, make sense of
body: Figurative: read a situation, a person's face, a map, a defense. Read someone's mind is fixed. (истолковывать, понимать, разгадывать)
examples: A good pitcher reads the batter's stance.
She read the room and dropped the subject.
We have read the market wrong twice this year.

senses.head: Come across a certain way
body: Intransitive, usually read as or read like: the impression a text or a person gives. No passive. (восприниматься, звучать (как))
examples: That line reads as sarcastic in print.
The apology read as insincere to everyone who saw it.

senses.head: Say, state (of a text)
body: Of a sign, label, or document — the wording is such-and-such. Takes no passive. (гласить, быть написанным)
examples: The sign reads 'No entry after six.'
The original draft read differently on that point.
The plaque had read 'Founded 1902' before someone repainted it.

senses.head: Show or take a reading
body: Works in both directions: the instrument reads a value, and a person reads the instrument. (показывать (о приборе); снимать показания)
examples: The gauge reads forty pounds.
The thermometer read ninety-eight at noon.
Someone from the utility has read the meter already.

senses.head: Retrieve data (computing)
body: Of drives, scanners, and programs. The opposite operation is write. (считывать (данные))
examples: The drive reads discs but won't burn them.
The scanner read the barcode on the second try.
The program has read the whole file into memory.

senses.head: read up on
body: Learn about a subject by reading, usually in preparation for something. (почитать о, изучить (тему))
examples: I need to read up on the new tax rules.
She read up on the company the night before the interview.
He has read up on every treatment option there is.

senses.head: read into
body: Find a meaning that may not be there. Usually negative: don't read too much into it. (домысливать, вкладывать смысл)
examples: Don't read too much into a one-word answer.
The press read a threat into a fairly bland statement.

senses.head: Study a subject (British)
body: British only, and formal even there: read history at Cambridge. Americans say majored in. (изучать, учиться (на факультете))
examples: She read law at Oxford in the eighties.
He has read classics for three years now.

entries.register: everyday — its irregularity is a trap for the ear, but the verb itself is basic
entries.third person: reads /ridz/ · -ing form: reading /ˈridɪŋ/ (both keep the REED vowel)
entries.contrast: This is the one verb in the group where the spelling lies. All three forms are read, but the past and the participle are pronounced /rɛd/, exactly like the color red: I read (REED) the news every morning against I read (RED) it yesterday. Only context or the speaker's voice separates them, and every prefixed form — reread, misread, proofread, sight-read — does the same thing.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the core senses; senses 4 and 5 (that line reads as sarcastic, the sign reads 'No entry after six') are stative — how a text stands, not something anyone does.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (I read two newspapers every morning), ditransitive (he read the kids a story), and intransitive in read as / read like and in she reads every night.
entries.passive: yes in the ordinary senses — the meter has been read already, the whole list had been read aloud. No in senses 4 and 5: ✗ sarcastic is read as by that line, ✗ 'No entry' is read by the sign.
entries.phrasal verbs: read back · read into · read off · read out · read over · read through · read up on

entries.meaning: To broadcast something a second time, or to relay a signal onward.
examples: The network plans to rebroadcast the finale on Sunday.
Public radio rebroadcast the interview the next morning.
The concert has been rebroadcast every December since 1998.
The tower rebroadcasts the signal to the far side of the valley.
The satellite had rebroadcast the feed to three continents before the outage.

senses.head: Air a program again
body: Follows broadcast; rebroadcasted is not standard. In everyday speech Americans say replay or air again. (повторно транслировать, давать в повторе)
examples: The network plans to rebroadcast the finale on Sunday.
Public radio rebroadcast the interview the next morning.
The concert has been rebroadcast every December since 1998.

senses.head: Relay a signal onward
body: Technical: a repeater or satellite picks up a signal and sends it out again. (ретранслировать (сигнал))
examples: The tower rebroadcasts the signal to the far side of the valley.
The satellite had rebroadcast the feed to three continents before the outage.

entries.register: rare — broadcast-industry word; ordinary speech says replay or air again
entries.contrast: Follows broadcast, and behind it cast; avoid rebroadcasted. In everyday American speech people usually say replay or air again.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; broadcast-industry vocabulary, where ordinary speech says replay or air again.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the program or the signal (the tower rebroadcasts the signal to the far side of the valley).
entries.passive: yes — the concert has been rebroadcast every December since 1998.

entries.meaning: To replace an actor in a role, to rework something into a new form, or to melt and mold metal again.
examples: Producers recast the role after two weeks of shooting.
The part has been recast twice since the read-through.
They may recast the lead if she drops out.
She recasts every complaint as a question.
He had recast the entire second act before opening night.
Let's recast this proposal in terms the board will understand.
The foundry recast the cracked bell in 1911.
The bronze has been recast three times over the centuries.

senses.head: Cast an actor again
body: Film and theater. Often passive — the part was recast — and never recasted. (переутверждать актёра, менять состав)
examples: Producers recast the role after two weeks of shooting.
The part has been recast twice since the read-through.
They may recast the lead if she drops out.

senses.head: Rework into a new form
body: Of an argument, a report, a policy: same material, different shape or framing. (переформулировать, преобразовывать, подавать по-новому)
examples: She recasts every complaint as a question.
He had recast the entire second act before opening night.
Let's recast this proposal in terms the board will understand.

senses.head: Melt down and mold again
body: Metalworking, from cast in its foundry sense. (переплавлять, отливать заново)
examples: The foundry recast the cracked bell in 1911.
The bronze has been recast three times over the centuries.

entries.register: neutral — ordinary in film talk and in editing prose, uncommon in conversation
entries.contrast: Two senses, one set of forms: replace an actor (the part was recast) and rework something in a new shape (she recast the argument in plain English). Both follow cast — never recasted.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: replacing an actor, reworking an argument, melting metal down again.
entries.transitivity: transitive — an actor, a proposal, or a casting (she recasts every complaint as a question).
entries.passive: yes, and it is usual in the film sense — the part has been recast twice since the read-through, the bronze has been recast three times over the centuries.

entries.meaning: To repair and re-equip something, especially a ship.
examples: The yard refits two ferries every winter.
They refitted the whole galley last spring.
The trawler has been refitted twice since it was launched.
It would cost more to refit the old plant than to build a new one.
The chain had refitted forty stores before the money ran out.
The mechanic refitted the panel and tightened every screw.
You will have to refit the door once the frame dries.

senses.head: Re-equip a ship or vehicle
body: The home sense. American English normally uses the regular refitted; the invariant refit is mostly the noun, stressed REE-fit. (переоборудовать, ремонтировать (судно))
examples: The yard refits two ferries every winter.
They refitted the whole galley last spring.
The trawler has been refitted twice since it was launched.

senses.head: Re-equip a building or plant
body: Chiefly British for shops and offices — the store closed for a refit. Americans say remodel or renovate. (переоснащать (помещение, завод))
examples: It would cost more to refit the old plant than to build a new one.
The chain had refitted forty stores before the money ran out.

senses.head: Put a part back on
body: Mechanical and everyday: fit again something that was removed. Refitted is the normal form here. (устанавливать обратно, ставить на место)
examples: The mechanic refitted the panel and tightened every screw.
You will have to refit the door once the frame dries.

entries.forms: refit /riˈfɪt/ · refit /riˈfɪt/ or refitted /riˈfɪtɪd/ · refit /riˈfɪt/ or refitted /riˈfɪtɪd/
entries.register: rare — nautical and engineering usage, and even there the noun is commoner
entries.contrast: American English normally uses the regular refitted — the ferry was refitted in 2019 — matching the fitted half of fit. The invariant refit is chiefly the noun: the ship went in for a refit, stressed REE-fit.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; American English normally uses the regular refitted, and the invariant refit is mostly the noun.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the ship, building, or part (the mechanic refitted the panel, the yard refits two ferries every winter).
entries.passive: yes — the trawler has been refitted twice since it was launched.

entries.meaning: To read something a second time, or to interpret a text in a new way.
examples: I reread (ree-REED) my favorite novel every summer.
She reread (ree-RED) the email four times before answering.
He has reread the contract and still has questions.
They had reread the instructions twice and were still stuck.
It helps to reread a hard paragraph out loud.
Later critics reread the novel as a book about class, not romance.
Historians have reread the whole decade in light of those letters.

senses.head: Read again
body: Follows read down to the vowel trap: ree-REED in the present, ree-RED in the past and participle. (перечитывать)
examples: I reread (ree-REED) my favorite novel every summer.
She reread (ree-RED) the email four times before answering.
He has reread the contract and still has questions.
They had reread the instructions twice and were still stuck.
It helps to reread a hard paragraph out loud.

senses.head: Reinterpret a text
body: Academic and critical writing: read something again and come out with a different reading of it. (переосмыслять, по-новому истолковывать)
examples: Later critics reread the novel as a book about class, not romance.
Historians have reread the whole decade in light of those letters.

entries.register: everyday — as ordinary as read, and used the same way
entries.third person: rereads /ˌriˈridz/ · -ing form: rereading /ˌriˈridɪŋ/ (both keep the REED vowel)
entries.contrast: Follows read exactly, pronunciation trap and all: I reread it last night is ree-RED, I reread it every summer is ree-REED.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, in both the literal and the critical sense.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she reread the email four times), intransitive when the object is obvious (it helps to reread a hard paragraph out loud).
entries.passive: yes — the novel has been reread as a book about class, not romance — though the active dominates.

entries.meaning: To return something to its starting state, or to set it again to a new value.
examples: Reset the router and try again.
I reset my password twice this morning and still can't get in.
The technician has reset every machine on the floor.
Somebody had reset the clock an hour ahead.
This switch resets the counter to zero.
We need to reset the thermostat for the weekend.
Both sides want to reset the relationship after the election.
The new coach reset expectations in his first week.
The surgeon reset the wrist under anesthesia.
The break had been reset badly the first time.

senses.head: Return to the starting state
body: The everyday sense, mostly of devices and accounts. Follows set, so never resetted. (сбрасывать, возвращать в исходное состояние)
examples: Reset the router and try again.
I reset my password twice this morning and still can't get in.
The technician has reset every machine on the floor.

senses.head: Set again to a new value
body: Of clocks, counters, thermostats, and traps — set once more, not necessarily back to zero. (переустанавливать, задавать заново)
examples: Somebody had reset the clock an hour ahead.
This switch resets the counter to zero.
We need to reset the thermostat for the weekend.

senses.head: Start over, wipe the slate
body: Figurative, common in politics and business. The noun is at least as common: a reset in relations. (начинать с чистого листа, перезапускать (отношения))
examples: Both sides want to reset the relationship after the election.
The new coach reset expectations in his first week.

senses.head: Set a broken bone again
body: Medical, and usually because the first attempt failed. (вправлять заново (кость))
examples: The surgeon reset the wrist under anesthesia.
The break had been reset badly the first time.

entries.register: everyday — routers, passwords, and relationships all get reset
entries.contrast: Follows set, so there is no resetted. The noun moves the stress forward — a hard REE-set — while the verb keeps it on the second syllable.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from routers and passwords to relationships and broken bones.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is what returns to its starting state (reset the router, this switch resets the counter to zero).
entries.passive: yes — every machine on the floor has been reset, the break had been reset badly the first time.

entries.meaning: To add new equipment or systems to something that was built without them.
examples: The city retrofits about a dozen schools a year.
They retrofitted the building with sprinklers in 2014.
Half the fleet has been retrofitted with cleaner engines.
It is cheaper to retrofit an old furnace than to replace it.
We had retrofitted the login system for two-factor before the audit.
Nobody wants to retrofit tests onto code this old.

senses.head: Add equipment to an existing structure
body: Engineering and construction. American writing strongly prefers the regular retrofitted. (модернизировать, дооснащать)
examples: The city retrofits about a dozen schools a year.
They retrofitted the building with sprinklers in 2014.
Half the fleet has been retrofitted with cleaner engines.

senses.head: Adapt an old design after the fact
body: Figurative, common in software: bolt a requirement onto a system that never anticipated it. (приспосабливать задним числом, дорабатывать)
examples: It is cheaper to retrofit an old furnace than to replace it.
We had retrofitted the login system for two-factor before the audit.
Nobody wants to retrofit tests onto code this old.

entries.forms: retrofit /ˈrɛtroʊˌfɪt/ · retrofit /ˈrɛtroʊˌfɪt/ or retrofitted /ˈrɛtroʊˌfɪtɪd/ · retrofit /ˈrɛtroʊˌfɪt/ or retrofitted /ˈrɛtroʊˌfɪtɪd/
entries.register: neutral — engineering, construction, and software writing; ordinary on the job
entries.contrast: American engineering writing uses the regular retrofitted far more than invariant retrofit — the bridge was retrofitted for earthquakes. That matches fit, where the "install" sense is also the regular one.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; American engineering writing strongly prefers the regular retrofitted.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the existing structure or system, usually with with (they retrofitted the building with sprinklers in 2014).
entries.passive: yes, and it is the common form — half the fleet has been retrofitted with cleaner engines.

entries.meaning: To free someone or something of something unwanted — almost always in rid X of Y, get rid of, or be rid of.
examples: I finally got rid of the old couch.
How do you get rid of fruit flies?
We got rid of almost everything in the garage last weekend.
Nothing will rid this basement of that smell.
The new manager rid the department of its worst habits.
He had rid himself of every reminder of the marriage.
I'm glad to be rid of that car.
She won't be rid of the paperwork until spring.

senses.head: get rid of
body: By far the commonest use of the word, and the one learners need first. Rid here is the participle after get. (избавиться от, выбросить)
examples: I finally got rid of the old couch.
How do you get rid of fruit flies?
We got rid of almost everything in the garage last weekend.

senses.head: rid X of Y
body: The full transitive frame, a shade formal. The reflexive rid oneself of is common in writing. (избавлять от, очищать от)
examples: Nothing will rid this basement of that smell.
The new manager rid the department of its worst habits.
He had rid himself of every reminder of the marriage.

senses.head: be rid of
body: A state rather than an action: get rid of is the doing, be rid of is the result. (быть свободным от, отделаться от)
examples: I'm glad to be rid of that car.
She won't be rid of the paperwork until spring.

entries.register: everyday — carried into daily speech by get rid of
entries.contrast: This verb almost never stands alone. It lives in rid X of Y — rid the house of mice — and in the fixed phrases get rid of and be rid of, where rid is the participle: I'm glad to be rid of it. Ridded exists but sounds strange to most Americans.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, but it barely stands alone: it lives in rid X of Y, in get rid of, and in the stative be rid of, which names the resulting state rather than the act.
entries.transitivity: transitive, and it demands an of-phrase: rid the basement of that smell, ✗ rid the basement. Often reflexive — he had rid himself of every reminder.
entries.passive: restricted — a true passive (the department was rid of its worst habits) is stiff and rare; what learners meet instead is get rid of and be rid of, fixed frames where rid is a participle but not a passive.

entries.meaning: To place something deliberately, to fix a value or state, or (of the sun) to go down — one of the busiest verbs in English.
examples: Set the box on the table by the door.
She set the tray down without a word.
They had set the table before the guests arrived.
The committee has set a deadline of March first.
The judge set bail at ten thousand dollars.
She set her alarm for five and still slept through it.
We need to set a price before Monday.
The sun set behind the ridge around eight.
The moon sets before midnight this week.
The sun had set by the time we reached the trailhead.
Let the concrete set overnight.
The gelatin set in about four hours.
The glue has set, so don't try to move it now.
She set a school record in the two hundred meter.
This decision sets a precedent nobody wants.
He has set the tone for the whole department.
The film is set in a small town in Maine.
They had set the whole play in a single room.
The foreman set two crews to work on the roof.
That remark set me thinking.
The noise has set the dogs barking.
Can you set up the projector before nine?
We set up the tent in the dark.
They have set up a fund for her medical bills.
They set off for the coast before dawn.
The smoke set off every alarm on the floor.
One comment has set off a week of arguing.
She set out to prove them all wrong.
The memo sets out three options.
He had set out the chairs an hour early.
The storm set the project back a month.
That repair set me back four hundred dollars.
Two recalls have set the company back years.
Set aside an hour for questions.
We set aside money every month for the trip.
The appeals court has set aside the verdict.

senses.head: Place something somewhere
body: The core sense, and it always takes an object. Sit is the one without an object: you sit down, but you set something down. ✗Set down and rest is dialect. (класть, ставить, помещать)
examples: Set the box on the table by the door.
She set the tray down without a word.
They had set the table before the guests arrived.

senses.head: Fix a time, price, or setting
body: Covers deadlines and prices as well as alarms, timers, and thermostats — anything given a value. (назначать, устанавливать, выставлять)
examples: The committee has set a deadline of March first.
The judge set bail at ten thousand dollars.
She set her alarm for five and still slept through it.
We need to set a price before Monday.

senses.head: Go down (of the sun)
body: The one common sense with no object at all. The opposite is rise. (садиться, заходить (о солнце, луне))
examples: The sun set behind the ridge around eight.
The moon sets before midnight this week.
The sun had set by the time we reached the trailhead.

senses.head: Become firm or solid
body: Intransitive, of concrete, glue, jelly, and plaster. (застывать, схватываться, твердеть)
examples: Let the concrete set overnight.
The gelatin set in about four hours.
The glue has set, so don't try to move it now.

senses.head: Establish a standard or record
body: Fixed collocations: set a record, set a precedent, set an example, set the tone. (устанавливать (рекорд), подавать (пример), задавать (тон))
examples: She set a school record in the two hundred meter.
This decision sets a precedent nobody wants.
He has set the tone for the whole department.

senses.head: Place a story in a time or place
body: Nearly always passive: the novel is set in 1930s Chicago. (помещать действие (в определённое время или место))
examples: The film is set in a small town in Maine.
They had set the whole play in a single room.

senses.head: Start someone or something going
body: Frames: set someone to work, set someone doing something, set something in motion. (заставлять, побуждать, пускать в ход)
examples: The foreman set two crews to work on the roof.
That remark set me thinking.
The noise has set the dogs barking.

senses.head: set up
body: Very common and broad: arrange, assemble, or establish something. It also means to frame someone: I was set up. (устраивать, налаживать, собирать; подставлять)
examples: Can you set up the projector before nine?
We set up the tent in the dark.
They have set up a fund for her medical bills.

senses.head: set off
body: Three uses that share a shape: depart, trigger an alarm or reaction, and detonate something. (отправляться; вызывать; приводить в действие)
examples: They set off for the coast before dawn.
The smoke set off every alarm on the floor.
One comment has set off a week of arguing.

senses.head: set out
body: Depart on a journey, state something in an orderly way, or lay items out. Set out to do something means to intend it. (отправляться в путь; излагать; выкладывать)
examples: She set out to prove them all wrong.
The memo sets out three options.
He had set out the chairs an hour early.

senses.head: set back
body: Delay progress, or — informally, always with a person and an amount — cost that much. (задерживать, отбрасывать назад; обойтись (в сумму))
examples: The storm set the project back a month.
That repair set me back four hundred dollars.
Two recalls have set the company back years.

senses.head: set aside
body: Reserve time or money, or — as a legal term — annul a verdict or ruling. (откладывать; отменять (решение))
examples: Set aside an hour for questions.
We set aside money every month for the trip.
The appeals court has set aside the verdict.

entries.register: everyday — one of the most-used verbs in the language, with senses in every domain
entries.contrast: Keep set apart from sit. Set takes an object — you set something down, set/set/set — while sit does not: you sit down, sit/sat/sat. ✗ Set down and rest is dialect, not standard. Every compound in this file — beset, inset, offset, reset, upset — copies set exactly.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; it also has a genuine intransitive life in the sun set and let the concrete set, where nothing is acted on at all.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive by default, and the object is obligatory, unlike sit: set the box on the table, ✗ set down and rest. Intransitive of the sun going down and of concrete, glue, or gelatin hardening.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the film is set in a small town in Maine, bail was set at ten thousand dollars. No passive for the sun or the concrete: ✗ the ridge was set behind by the sun.
entries.phrasal verbs: set about · set apart · set aside · set back · set down · set forth · set in · set off · set out · set to · set up · set upon
entries.see also: put, let, reset, offset, inset, upset, beset

entries.meaning: To let something fall away — leaves, hair, tears, weight, or a burden.
examples: Our dog sheds year round.
The maples shed their leaves early that year.
That snake has shed twice this spring.
He has shed twenty pounds since January.
The company shed four hundred jobs last quarter.
She had shed the last of her doubts by the second interview.
They shed a few tears at the airport and then laughed about it.
Nobody wants to shed blood over a parking space.
Plenty of blood had been shed over that border already.
The new emails shed light on who knew what.
Her testimony has shed light on a very murky deal.
This jacket sheds rain but not wind.
The tarp shed water all night without leaking.

senses.head: Drop hair, skin, or leaves
body: The literal sense, of animals and plants. No shedded. (линять, сбрасывать (шерсть, листву, кожу))
examples: Our dog sheds year round.
The maples shed their leaves early that year.
That snake has shed twice this spring.

senses.head: Lose or get rid of
body: Of weight, jobs, costs, doubts — anything a person or an organization drops on purpose. (сбрасывать (вес), избавляться от)
examples: He has shed twenty pounds since January.
The company shed four hundred jobs last quarter.
She had shed the last of her doubts by the second interview.

senses.head: shed tears, shed blood
body: Fixed and slightly formal. Often passive in the negative: not a tear was shed. (проливать (слёзы, кровь))
examples: They shed a few tears at the airport and then laughed about it.
Nobody wants to shed blood over a parking space.
Plenty of blood had been shed over that border already.

senses.head: shed light on
body: Fixed idiom: make something clearer, usually a question or a mystery. (проливать свет на)
examples: The new emails shed light on who knew what.
Her testimony has shed light on a very murky deal.

senses.head: Repel water
body: Of coatings, fabrics, and roofs: water runs off instead of soaking in. (не пропускать (воду), отталкивать)
examples: This jacket sheds rain but not wind.
The tarp shed water all night without leaking.

entries.register: everyday — dogs shed, companies shed jobs, and evidence sheds light
entries.contrast: Don't mix it up with shred, a different verb one letter away. No shedded: the dog shed all over the couch last night.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 5 (this jacket sheds rain but not wind) states a standing property rather than an event.
entries.transitivity: transitive — hair, leaves, weight, jobs, tears, blood, or water (the company shed four hundred jobs last quarter).
entries.passive: yes — plenty of blood had been shed over that border already, not a tear was shed. The idiom shed light on stays active.

entries.meaning: To empty the bowels — vulgar — plus a handful of vulgar idioms built on the same verb.
examples: The dog shit on the neighbor's lawn again last night.
Don't let the puppy shit in the house.
A raccoon has shit in the crawlspace.
They shit on their own staff for years.
Nobody deserves to be shit on like that.
He has shit on every partner he ever had.
I nearly shit myself when the alarm went off.
Half the office had shit a brick over the audit before anyone read the findings.

senses.head: Empty the bowels
body: Vulgar; keep it out of writing that matters. The past is genuinely unsettled — shit, shat, and shitted all occur, with shit commonest and shat usually played for laughs. (испражняться, гадить)
examples: The dog shit on the neighbor's lawn again last night.
Don't let the puppy shit in the house.
A raccoon has shit in the crawlspace.

senses.head: shit on someone
body: Vulgar: treat someone with contempt, or badmouth them. Common in the passive. (обходиться по-свински, унижать)
examples: They shit on their own staff for years.
Nobody deserves to be shit on like that.
He has shit on every partner he ever had.

senses.head: shit oneself, shit a brick
body: Vulgar fixed phrases for sudden terror. Rarely literal. (перепугаться до смерти)
examples: I nearly shit myself when the alarm went off.
Half the office had shit a brick over the audit before anyone read the findings.

entries.forms: shit /ʃɪt/ · shit /ʃɪt/ or shat /ʃæt/ · shit /ʃɪt/ or shat /ʃæt/
entries.register: vulgar — ordinary in rough speech, barred from writing that matters
entries.contrast: Vulgar — keep it out of writing that matters. Its past forms are genuinely unsettled: American speakers say shit, shat, and shitted, with shit the commonest and shat used mostly for comic effect. Dictionaries list all three.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and vulgar; barred from writing that matters.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in the literal sense (the dog shit on the neighbor's lawn), transitive in the fixed shit oneself and shit a brick, and prepositional in shit on someone.
entries.passive: restricted — only the prepositional passive works: nobody deserves to be shit on like that. The literal intransitive has no passive.

entries.meaning: To cut or tear something into strips, literally or figuratively.
examples: Shred the cheese while the pasta boils.
He shredded every statement before recycling it.
The office has shredded six boxes of old files.
The defense shredded the witness's timeline.
Her testimony had shredded the company's whole story by lunch.
The flag had shredded in the wind by the end of the week.
Cheap tires shred on gravel roads.
That kid can really shred.
They shredded the back bowls all afternoon.

senses.head: Cut into strips
body: Ordinary American English treats this as a regular verb — shredded — even though dictionaries list the invariant form. (измельчать, шинковать, рвать на полоски)
examples: Shred the cheese while the pasta boils.
He shredded every statement before recycling it.
The office has shredded six boxes of old files.

senses.head: Demolish an argument
body: Figurative, of testimony, a theory, or a defense. (разносить в клочья, разбивать (доводы))
examples: The defense shredded the witness's timeline.
Her testimony had shredded the company's whole story by lunch.

senses.head: Come apart in strips
body: Intransitive, of fabric, tires, and paper. (расползаться, изнашиваться в лохмотья)
examples: The flag had shredded in the wind by the end of the week.
Cheap tires shred on gravel roads.

senses.head: Play or ride brilliantly
body: American slang, from guitar solos and from skiing and skateboarding. Often intransitive. (круто играть (на гитаре), лихо кататься)
examples: That kid can really shred.
They shredded the back bowls all afternoon.

entries.forms: shred /ʃrɛd/ · shred /ʃrɛd/ or shredded /ˈʃrɛdɪd/ · shred /ʃrɛd/ or shredded /ˈʃrɛdɪd/
entries.register: everyday — documents, cheese, and tires all shred in ordinary use
entries.contrast: Ordinary American English treats this as a regular verb: she shredded the documents, the tires had shredded. The invariant shred is listed in some sources but sounds wrong in most sentences. Also keep it apart from shed.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; American English treats it as a regular verb (shredded) in nearly every sentence.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive of documents, cheese, or an argument (the defense shredded the witness's timeline), intransitive of fabric and tires coming apart (cheap tires shred on gravel roads) and of the slang that kid can really shred.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — six boxes of old files have been shredded. The intransitive coming-apart and slang senses have none.

entries.meaning: To move something into a closed position, and the base of several very common phrasal verbs.
examples: Please shut the window — it's freezing.
He shut the door harder than he meant to.
She shut her eyes and counted to ten.
They have shut the plant for two weeks of maintenance.
The diner shuts at nine on weeknights.
The store had shut by the time we got downtown.
The company shut down two plants last year.
Shut down the laptop before you unplug it.
Protests have shut down the interstate twice this month.
The city shut off the water at eight.
Shut off the burner when it starts to steam.
Somebody had shut off the alarm during the night.
He told them to shut up, which did not help.
She shut up the second her boss walked in.
The dog had been shut up in the garage all afternoon.
Heavy curtains shut out most of the street noise.
The rookie shut out the Yankees for seven innings.
New rules have shut small growers out of the market.

senses.head: Close something
body: Blunter than close, and it will not sit in front of a noun: a closed door, not ✗a shut door. (закрывать)
examples: Please shut the window — it's freezing.
He shut the door harder than he meant to.
She shut her eyes and counted to ten.

senses.head: Close for business
body: Of stores, plants, and offices, temporarily or for good. (закрывать(ся) (о заведении))
examples: They have shut the plant for two weeks of maintenance.
The diner shuts at nine on weeknights.
The store had shut by the time we got downtown.

senses.head: shut down
body: Close an operation permanently, halt an activity, or power a machine off. Also of a person: he shut down means he stopped responding. (закрывать, останавливать; выключать)
examples: The company shut down two plants last year.
Shut down the laptop before you unplug it.
Protests have shut down the interstate twice this month.

senses.head: shut off
body: Stop a flow — water, gas, power — or cut something off from access. (перекрывать, отключать)
examples: The city shut off the water at eight.
Shut off the burner when it starts to steam.
Somebody had shut off the alarm during the night.

senses.head: shut up
body: Rude as an order. The second, older sense is to lock someone or something away: shut up in a room. (замолчать, заткнуться; запирать)
examples: He told them to shut up, which did not help.
She shut up the second her boss walked in.
The dog had been shut up in the garage all afternoon.

senses.head: shut out
body: Keep something outside, exclude someone, or — in baseball and hockey — hold the other side scoreless. (не впускать, отгораживаться; сыграть всухую)
examples: Heavy curtains shut out most of the street noise.
The rookie shut out the Yankees for seven innings.
New rules have shut small growers out of the market.

entries.register: everyday — a core verb, blunter than close but just as common
entries.contrast: Shut and close mean the same thing, but shut is blunter and will not sit in front of a noun: a closed door, not ✗ a shut door. And shut up means "be quiet," which is rude.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; unlike close it will not stand in front of a noun as an adjective: a closed door, ✗ a shut door.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (shut the window, they shut down two plants), intransitive of a business closing (the diner shuts at nine on weeknights).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the interstate has been shut down twice this month, the dog had been shut up in the garage all afternoon.
entries.phrasal verbs: shut away · shut down · shut off · shut out · shut up

entries.meaning: To play or sing music from a score you have never seen before.
examples: Good accompanists sight-read almost anything.
She sight-read the whole sonata at the audition.
He has sight-read for that choir for years.
They had sight-read the part once and then recorded it.
You have to practice to sight-read well.

senses.head: Play music at first sight
body: Music only, and a real skill rather than a casual act. Follows read in pronunciation: the past and participle are said SITE-red. (играть или петь с листа (по нотам))
examples: Good accompanists sight-read almost anything.
She sight-read the whole sonata at the audition.
He has sight-read for that choir for years.
They had sight-read the part once and then recorded it.
You have to practice to sight-read well.

entries.русский: играть или петь с листа (по нотам)
entries.register: rare — musicians' vocabulary and nothing else
entries.third person: sight-reads /ˈsaɪtˌridz/ · -ing form: sight-reading /ˈsaɪtˌridɪŋ/ (both keep the REED vowel)
entries.contrast: Follows read, pronunciation shift included: she sight-read the piece cold is SITE-red.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a musician's skill word and nothing else.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the music as object (she sight-read the whole sonata at the audition), intransitive of the ability itself (you have to practice to sight-read well).
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical (the part had been sight-read once and then recorded) but rare, since the performer is normally the subject.

entries.meaning: To carry the same program on two channels or media at the same time.
examples: The station simulcasts the game on AM and FM.
They simulcast the ceremony on three platforms last May.
The network had simulcast the address in Spanish as well.
The track simulcasts races from six other venues.
The concert has been simulcast to theaters nationwide.
We plan to simulcast the keynote to every regional office.

senses.head: Broadcast on two channels at once
body: A blend of simultaneous and broadcast, and it inherits the invariance: never simulcasted. (транслировать одновременно (по радио и телевидению))
examples: The station simulcasts the game on AM and FM.
They simulcast the ceremony on three platforms last May.
The network had simulcast the address in Spanish as well.

senses.head: Send a live event to other venues
body: Common in horse racing, cinema, and corporate events: one live feed shown in many rooms at once. (транслировать в прямом эфире на другие площадки)
examples: The track simulcasts races from six other venues.
The concert has been simulcast to theaters nationwide.
We plan to simulcast the keynote to every regional office.

entries.register: rare — a broadcast-industry blend, at home in racing and cinema listings
entries.contrast: A blend of simultaneous and broadcast, and it inherits the invariance along with the forms: never simulcasted.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a blend of simultaneous and broadcast that inherits both the forms and the sense.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the program or event (the station simulcasts the game on AM and FM).
entries.passive: yes — the concert has been simulcast to theaters nationwide.

entries.meaning: To make a long, narrow cut in something.
examples: Slit the bag open along the top.
He slit the envelope with a kitchen knife.
Someone has slit the seam on this cushion.
This blade slits plastic wrap cleanly.
He threatened to slit the man's throat.
The animal's throat had been slit cleanly.

senses.head: Cut a long narrow opening
body: One straight cut, not a break into pieces — that is split, one letter away. (разрезать вдоль, делать надрез)
examples: Slit the bag open along the top.
He slit the envelope with a kitchen knife.
Someone has slit the seam on this cushion.
This blade slits plastic wrap cleanly.

senses.head: Slit a throat or wrists
body: Nearly fixed collocations, and the sense most people meet first: slit someone's throat, slit his wrists. Often passive. (перерезать (горло, вены))
examples: He threatened to slit the man's throat.
The animal's throat had been slit cleanly.

entries.register: neutral — ordinary in narrative writing, mostly in slit open and slit a throat
entries.contrast: Slit and split are one letter apart and easy to confuse: a slit is one long narrow cut, a split is a break into separate parts.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and sudden: one long narrow cut, not a break into parts.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is obligatory (slit the bag open along the top, this blade slits plastic wrap cleanly).
entries.passive: yes — the animal's throat had been slit cleanly, someone has slit the seam on this cushion.

entries.meaning: To break or divide something into parts, to share something out, or — in slang — to leave.
examples: Let's split the check.
We split the last piece of pie three ways.
That firm splits profits evenly among the partners.
He split a stack of firewood before breakfast.
The log had split along an old crack.
The seam has split on both sides.
The party has split into two camps.
The vote split the town down the middle.
A single issue can split a coalition in a week.
They split up after eleven years.
Let's split up and cover both entrances.
Two of my cousins have split up this year.
We split around midnight.
He had split before the police arrived.
We split the difference and settled at nine thousand.
They have split the difference on every contract so far.
Don't split hairs — you know what I meant.
The committee split hairs for two hours over one word.
The stock split two for one in June.
The company has split its shares three times since 2010.

senses.head: Divide into parts, share out
body: The commonest sense. No splitted, ever. (делить, разделять (поровну))
examples: Let's split the check.
We split the last piece of pie three ways.
That firm splits profits evenly among the partners.

senses.head: Break or crack along a line
body: Works with or without an object. The -ing form as an adjective means severe: a splitting headache. (раскалывать(ся), расщеплять(ся), лопаться)
examples: He split a stack of firewood before breakfast.
The log had split along an old crack.
The seam has split on both sides.

senses.head: Divide into opposing groups
body: Of parties, committees, congregations, and towns. (раскалывать (группу), разделяться)
examples: The party has split into two camps.
The vote split the town down the middle.
A single issue can split a coalition in a week.

senses.head: split up
body: End a relationship, or divide people into smaller groups. (расставаться, разводиться; разбиваться на группы)
examples: They split up after eleven years.
Let's split up and cover both entrances.
Two of my cousins have split up this year.

senses.head: Leave, take off
body: Informal American slang, a little dated but still understood. (сваливать, уходить)
examples: We split around midnight.
He had split before the police arrived.

senses.head: split the difference
body: Fixed phrase from bargaining: settle halfway between two numbers. (сойтись на середине, поделить разницу)
examples: We split the difference and settled at nine thousand.
They have split the difference on every contract so far.

senses.head: split hairs
body: Fixed idiom, always critical: argue over distinctions too fine to matter. (придираться к мелочам, спорить о пустяках)
examples: Don't split hairs — you know what I meant.
The committee split hairs for two hours over one word.

senses.head: Split shares (finance)
body: A company divides each share into several, lowering the price per share. (дробить (акции))
examples: The stock split two for one in June.
The company has split its shares three times since 2010.

entries.register: everyday — bills, parties, and firewood all get split in ordinary speech
entries.contrast: No splitted. Two side notes: split meaning "leave" is slang — we split around midnight — and splitting as an adjective means severe: a splitting headache. Compare slit, which is a narrow cut rather than a break.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the -ing form is an intensifying adjective in a splitting headache.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (let's split the check, the vote split the town down the middle), intransitive of something breaking or people parting (the log had split along an old crack, they split up after eleven years).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — profits are split evenly among the partners, the difference has been split. No passive for the slang we split around midnight.
entries.phrasal verbs: split off · split on · split up

entries.meaning: To cover or reach a wider area, or to move something out across a surface.
examples: The fire spread faster than anyone expected.
The virus has spread to eleven counties.
By dawn the oil had spread across the whole harbor.
She spreads peanut butter on everything.
Spread the frosting while the cake is still warm.
He spread butter on both halves.
Spread the blanket over there, in the shade.
They spread a map across the hood of the truck.
The bird had spread its wings to dry.
Rumors spread through a small town in hours.
Someone has spread the news already.
Please don't spread this around.
We spread the payments over eighteen months.
The dentist has spread the work across three visits.
Spread out so everyone can see.
The searchers spread out along the riverbank.
She has spread herself too thin this semester.
He spread himself too thin and finished nothing.

senses.head: Extend over a wider area
body: Of fire, disease, news, and influence. The vowel never changes — spread rhymes with bed in all three forms, and there is no spreaded. (распространяться, расширяться)
examples: The fire spread faster than anyone expected.
The virus has spread to eleven counties.
By dawn the oil had spread across the whole harbor.

senses.head: Apply something soft to a surface
body: Butter, frosting, glue, mortar. The noun a spread is the thing you put on bread. (намазывать)
examples: She spreads peanut butter on everything.
Spread the frosting while the cake is still warm.
He spread butter on both halves.

senses.head: Open something out flat
body: Of blankets, maps, wings, and arms. (расстилать, раскладывать, расправлять)
examples: Spread the blanket over there, in the shade.
They spread a map across the hood of the truck.
The bird had spread its wings to dry.

senses.head: Pass information around
body: Spread the word and spread a rumor are both fixed. Often disapproving. (распространять (слухи, новости))
examples: Rumors spread through a small town in hours.
Someone has spread the news already.
Please don't spread this around.

senses.head: Distribute over time or people
body: Usually spread over or spread across: payments, work, risk. (распределять, растягивать (во времени))
examples: We spread the payments over eighteen months.
The dentist has spread the work across three visits.

senses.head: spread out
body: Of people moving apart to cover more ground. (рассредоточиваться, расходиться)
examples: Spread out so everyone can see.
The searchers spread out along the riverbank.

senses.head: spread oneself too thin
body: Fixed idiom: take on so much that nothing gets proper attention. (разбрасываться, браться за слишком многое)
examples: She has spread herself too thin this semester.
He spread himself too thin and finished nothing.

entries.register: everyday — of fire, news, butter, and blankets alike
entries.contrast: Watch the vowel, because it is the mirror image of read: spread rhymes with bed in all three forms and never changes its sound. And there is no spreaded.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both directions: something spreads on its own, or somebody spreads it.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive of fire, disease, and rumors (the fire spread faster than anyone expected), transitive of butter, blankets, news, and payments (we spread the payments over eighteen months).
entries.passive: yes for the transitive senses — the news has been spread already, the work has been spread across three visits. No for the intransitive: ✗ eleven counties have been spread to by the virus.

entries.meaning: To rent out to someone else a place you are renting yourself.
examples: Many students sublet their apartments over the summer.
He sublet his studio to a friend while he was in Chicago.
She has sublet the same one-bedroom three years running.
My lease says I can't sublet at all.
We sublet a place near campus for three months last fall.
They had sublet the unit from a graduate student who never told the landlord.
The builder sublets the electrical work.
Most of the finish work had been sublet to a smaller firm.

senses.head: Rent out your rental
body: Forms come from let in its "rent out" sense — no subletted. The noun pulls the stress forward: a summer SUB-let. (сдавать в субаренду, пересдавать)
examples: Many students sublet their apartments over the summer.
He sublet his studio to a friend while he was in Chicago.
She has sublet the same one-bedroom three years running.
My lease says I can't sublet at all.

senses.head: Take a place on a sublease
body: Speakers use the verb in both directions; only context tells you who is renting from whom. (снимать в субаренду)
examples: We sublet a place near campus for three months last fall.
They had sublet the unit from a graduate student who never told the landlord.

senses.head: Subcontract work
body: Chiefly British construction usage; Americans say subcontract or sub out. (передавать работы субподрядчику)
examples: The builder sublets the electrical work.
Most of the finish work had been sublet to a smaller firm.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary for anyone who rents, and standard on a lease
entries.contrast: Forms come from let in its "rent out" sense — no subletted. The noun pulls the stress to the front: she found a summer SUB-let.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; it takes its forms and its meaning from let in the rent-out sense.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he sublet his studio to a friend), intransitive when the practice itself is meant (my lease says I can't sublet at all).
entries.passive: yes — most of the finish work had been sublet to a smaller firm.

entries.meaning: To give off moisture through the skin, and by extension to worry or to work very hard.
examples: I sweat buckets on that hike last August.
He sweats through a shirt just walking to the subway.
The pitcher had sweat right through his cap by the fourth inning.
Don't sweat the small stuff.
She has sweat over this presentation for a week.
They sweated over that budget for a month.
He has sweat blood for this company.
We had to sweat it out until the results came back.
We sweated out the last ten minutes of the game.
The glass sweats in this humidity.
The basement walls had sweat all through July.
Sweat the onions in butter for about five minutes.
He sweated the leeks before adding the stock.

senses.head: Perspire
body: American writing prefers the invariant sweat, British writing sweated; both are standard. The vowel rhymes with bet, not beat. (потеть)
examples: I sweat buckets on that hike last August.
He sweats through a shirt just walking to the subway.
The pitcher had sweat right through his cap by the fourth inning.

senses.head: Worry, be anxious
body: Most often in the fixed negatives don't sweat it and don't sweat the small stuff. (переживать, нервничать)
examples: Don't sweat the small stuff.
She has sweat over this presentation for a week.

senses.head: Work very hard
body: Usually sweat over something, or the fixed sweat blood. (вкалывать, трудиться до седьмого пота)
examples: They sweated over that budget for a month.
He has sweat blood for this company.

senses.head: sweat it out
body: Wait through something unpleasant with no way to speed it up. (вытерпеть, дождаться исхода)
examples: We had to sweat it out until the results came back.
We sweated out the last ten minutes of the game.

senses.head: Give off moisture (of things)
body: Of a cold glass, a block of cheese, or a basement wall in humid weather. (запотевать, отпотевать, отсыревать)
examples: The glass sweats in this humidity.
The basement walls had sweat all through July.

senses.head: Cook gently in fat
body: Cooking term: cook vegetables soft over low heat without letting them brown. (пассеровать, томить (овощи))
examples: Sweat the onions in butter for about five minutes.
He sweated the leeks before adding the stock.

entries.forms: sweat /swɛt/ · sweat /swɛt/ or sweated /ˈswɛtɪd/ · sweat /swɛt/ or sweated /ˈswɛtɪd/
entries.register: everyday — literal and figurative both, as in don't sweat it
entries.third person: sweats · -ing form: sweating (no doubling — two vowel letters before the t)
entries.contrast: Both forms are standard. American writing prefers the invariant sweat — I sweat through my shirt — while British writing prefers sweated. Note the vowel too: sweat rhymes with bet, not with beat.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, though perspiring is a bodily process rather than a chosen act; it takes the progressive freely (he's sweating through his shirt).
entries.transitivity: both — mostly intransitive (I sweat buckets on that hike, the glass sweats in this humidity), transitive in don't sweat it, sweat blood, sweat it out, and the cooking sweat the onions in butter.
entries.passive: restricted — only the cooking sense passivizes naturally (the leeks were sweated before the stock went in); the idioms refuse it (✗ the small stuff shouldn't be sweated) and the intransitive has no passive.

entries.meaning: To broadcast something on television.
examples: CBS telecasts the tournament every April.
The network telecast the moon landing to sixty countries.
The game has been telecast in prime time twice this season.
The ceremony had been telecast live before the tape was lost.
They will telecast the final round on Sunday.

senses.head: Broadcast on television
body: A dated word — American English now says broadcast, air, or televise. Forms follow cast, so never telecasted. (передавать по телевидению, транслировать)
examples: CBS telecasts the tournament every April.
The network telecast the moon landing to sixty countries.
The game has been telecast in prime time twice this season.
The ceremony had been telecast live before the tape was lost.
They will telecast the final round on Sunday.

entries.register: dated — the industry's old word; American English now says broadcast or air
entries.contrast: A dated word — American English now just says broadcast or air. Forms follow cast, so no telecasted.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and dated; American English now says broadcast, air, or televise.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the program or event (CBS telecasts the tournament every April).
entries.passive: yes — the game has been telecast in prime time twice this season, the ceremony had been telecast live.

entries.meaning: To push something forward suddenly and hard, or to force someone into a situation.
examples: He thrust his hands into his pockets and said nothing.
She thrusts her chin out whenever she is challenged.
Don't thrust the pole any deeper — you'll hit the line.
The accident has thrust the mayor into a fight she never wanted.
History had thrust an ordinary man into an impossible job.
She was thrust into the lead role two days before opening.
They thrust the job on him and then complained about how he did it.
No one should have that kind of responsibility thrust upon them at nineteen.
He thrust the blade forward and missed.
The two fencers have thrust and parried for an hour.
A rock ledge thrusts out over the valley.
The pier thrust two hundred feet into the lake.

senses.head: Push forcefully
body: The literal sense, always sudden and usually with a direction word: into, forward, out. No thrusted in careful writing. (толкать, всовывать, вонзать)
examples: He thrust his hands into his pockets and said nothing.
She thrusts her chin out whenever she is challenged.
Don't thrust the pole any deeper — you'll hit the line.

senses.head: Force into a role (passive)
body: be thrust into is the commonest frame in modern prose, and it always implies the person did not choose it. (ввергать, бросать (в ситуацию, на роль))
examples: The accident has thrust the mayor into a fight she never wanted.
History had thrust an ordinary man into an impossible job.
She was thrust into the lead role two days before opening.

senses.head: Force something on someone
body: thrust something on or upon someone — slightly formal, always unwelcome. (навязывать)
examples: They thrust the job on him and then complained about how he did it.
No one should have that kind of responsibility thrust upon them at nineteen.

senses.head: Stab, lunge
body: Fencing and hand-to-hand combat, and the source of the noun a thrust. (делать выпад, наносить колющий удар)
examples: He thrust the blade forward and missed.
The two fencers have thrust and parried for an hour.

senses.head: Jut out, protrude
body: Of cliffs, piers, and towers — the shape of a sudden push, held still. (выдаваться, выступать)
examples: A rock ledge thrusts out over the valley.
The pier thrust two hundred feet into the lake.

entries.register: neutral — common in narrative and technical writing, rare in conversation
entries.contrast: No thrusted in careful writing. The commonest pattern is the passive with into: she was thrust into a job nobody wanted.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and sudden; sense 5 (a rock ledge thrusts out over the valley) is stative — the shape of a push, held still.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a direction phrase (he thrust his hands into his pockets), intransitive in the fencing and protruding senses (the pier thrust two hundred feet into the lake).
entries.passive: yes, and be thrust into is the commonest frame of all — she was thrust into the lead role two days before opening, responsibility thrust upon them at nineteen.

entries.meaning: To keep casting an actor in the same kind of role, or to label a person by one trait.
examples: Hollywood typecasts character actors within about two films.
That single role typecast him for twenty years.
She has been typecast as the tough boss in every series since.
It is hard not to typecast someone you have only seen in one job.
The industry had typecast him long before he noticed.

senses.head: Cast in the same kind of role
body: Nearly always passive: he was typecast as the villain. Forms follow cast; typecasted is not standard. (утверждать на однотипные роли, эксплуатировать типаж)
examples: Hollywood typecasts character actors within about two films.
That single role typecast him for twenty years.
She has been typecast as the tough boss in every series since.

senses.head: Pigeonhole a person
body: Outside acting: judge someone by one visible trait or one job they once had. (навешивать ярлык, загонять в рамки)
examples: It is hard not to typecast someone you have only seen in one job.
The industry had typecast him long before he noticed.

entries.register: neutral — entertainment talk and its figurative extension; ordinary in writing
entries.contrast: Nearly always passive — he was typecast as the villain. Forms follow cast; typecasted is not standard.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and met almost entirely as a passive participle.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the actor or the person being labeled (Hollywood typecasts character actors within about two films).
entries.passive: yes, and it is the default — he was typecast as the villain, she has been typecast as the tough boss in every series since.

entries.meaning: To sell more cheaply than a rival, or to weaken something from underneath.
examples: Their online store undercuts every shop in town.
The importer undercut local growers by thirty percent.
Cheap imports have undercut the whole industry.
His own memo has undercut everything he said in the meeting.
Two earlier rulings had undercut the state's argument.
Don't undercut your own case with a joke.
The river had undercut the bank until the tree fell in.
The mason undercuts the joint so the mortar holds.

senses.head: Sell below a competitor
body: Business. The verb is stressed un-dur-KUT; the noun an UN-dur-cut moves the stress forward. (сбивать цену, продавать дешевле конкурентов)
examples: Their online store undercuts every shop in town.
The importer undercut local growers by thirty percent.
Cheap imports have undercut the whole industry.

senses.head: Weaken, undermine
body: Figurative: take the support out from under an argument, a policy, or a person. (подрывать, ослаблять)
examples: His own memo has undercut everything he said in the meeting.
Two earlier rulings had undercut the state's argument.
Don't undercut your own case with a joke.

senses.head: Cut away from underneath
body: Literal, in carpentry, masonry, and geology — a river undercuts a bank until it collapses. (подрезать снизу, подмывать)
examples: The river had undercut the bank until the tree fell in.
The mason undercuts the joint so the mortar holds.

entries.register: neutral — business and policy writing, and ordinary on the job
entries.contrast: The stress moves with the part of speech: the verb is un-dur-KUT, the noun UN-dur-kut. Forms come from cut.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: pricing, undermining, and cutting away from below.
entries.transitivity: transitive — a rival, an argument, or a riverbank (their online store undercuts every shop in town).
entries.passive: yes — the whole industry has been undercut by cheap imports, the bank had been undercut until the tree fell in.

entries.meaning: To hit someone with a short upward punch from below.
examples: He uppercuts whenever his opponent drops a shoulder.
She uppercut him twice in the final round.
The champion has uppercut his way out of trouble before.
By the eighth the challenger had uppercut him into the ropes.
You can't uppercut from that far away.

senses.head: Punch upward from below
body: Boxing shorthand. The noun — a left uppercut — is far commoner than the verb. Forms follow cut. (бить апперкотом, наносить апперкот)
examples: He uppercuts whenever his opponent drops a shoulder.
She uppercut him twice in the final round.
The champion has uppercut his way out of trouble before.
By the eighth the challenger had uppercut him into the ropes.
You can't uppercut from that far away.

entries.register: rare — boxing shorthand, and even there the noun does nearly all the work
entries.contrast: The noun — a left uppercut — is far commoner than the verb, which is boxing shorthand. Forms follow cut.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; boxing shorthand, and the noun a left uppercut does nearly all the work.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the opponent as object (she uppercut him twice in the final round), intransitive of the technique (he uppercuts whenever his opponent drops a shoulder).
entries.passive: restricted — buildable but almost never written (he was uppercut into the ropes); boxing writing keeps the puncher as the subject.

entries.meaning: To make someone unhappy, to knock something over, or to beat a favorite.
examples: It upsets her when people are late.
The email upset him more than he let on.
Try not to upset the baby right before a nap.
Rich food has upset my stomach all week.
The medication upset his stomach for two days.
He upset an entire tray of glasses.
The cat has upset the water bowl twice today.
Careful — you'll upset the whole board.
A tenth seed had upset the champion in the first round.
An unknown candidate upset the incumbent by four points.
The strike upset our whole delivery schedule.
One late shipment can upset the balance for a month.
The ruling has upset decades of settled practice.

senses.head: Make someone unhappy
body: The everyday sense. The participle doubles as an adjective — he looked upset — and is stressed up-SET, while the noun an UP-set moves the stress forward. (расстраивать, огорчать)
examples: It upsets her when people are late.
The email upset him more than he let on.
Try not to upset the baby right before a nap.

senses.head: Disturb the stomach
body: Fixed collocation: upset someone's stomach, and the adjective an upset stomach. (расстраивать (желудок))
examples: Rich food has upset my stomach all week.
The medication upset his stomach for two days.

senses.head: Knock something over
body: The oldest sense and still current, though knock over is commoner in speech. (опрокидывать)
examples: He upset an entire tray of glasses.
The cat has upset the water bowl twice today.
Careful — you'll upset the whole board.

senses.head: Beat a favorite
body: Sports and politics. The noun is even commoner: a major upset. (неожиданно побеждать фаворита)
examples: A tenth seed had upset the champion in the first round.
An unknown candidate upset the incumbent by four points.

senses.head: Disrupt a plan or balance
body: Of schedules, ecosystems, and settled arrangements. (нарушать (планы, равновесие))
examples: The strike upset our whole delivery schedule.
One late shipment can upset the balance for a month.
The ruling has upset decades of settled practice.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: The verb and the participle-adjective are stressed up-SET; the noun — a major UP-set — moves the stress forward. Forms follow set, so never upsetted.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and causative (it upsets her when people are late); the participle is a true adjective in he looked upset, stressed up-SET.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the person, the stomach, the thing knocked over, the favorite, or the plan (a tenth seed had upset the champion).
entries.passive: yes — the incumbent was upset by an unknown candidate, decades of settled practice have been upset. Note that she was upset is usually the adjective, not a passive.

entries.meaning: To marry someone, to perform a marriage, or to join two things closely together.
examples: They wed in a courthouse ceremony last fall.
