The couple weds on Saturday.
By then he had wed twice and divorced once.
They plan to wed in the spring.
The same judge wed both of my sisters.
A retired chaplain has wedded half the couples in that town.
A good design weds comfort to durability.
The album wedded country lyrics to a punk rhythm section.
She has wedded herself to a theory the data doesn't support.
He is too wedded to the old process to see the problem.

senses.head: Marry, get married
body: Formal or headline English — Couple weds after 40 years. In plain speech Americans say get married. Both wed and wedded are standard pasts. (жениться, выходить замуж)
examples: They wed in a courthouse ceremony last fall.
The couple weds on Saturday.
By then he had wed twice and divorced once.
They plan to wed in the spring.

senses.head: Perform a marriage
body: Transitive, with the officiant as the subject: a judge or minister weds the couple. (венчать, женить, сочетать браком)
examples: The same judge wed both of my sisters.
A retired chaplain has wedded half the couples in that town.

senses.head: Join two things closely
body: Figurative and a little literary: wed X to Y, of styles, ideas, or qualities. (соединять, сочетать)
examples: A good design weds comfort to durability.
The album wedded country lyrics to a punk rhythm section.

senses.head: be wedded to an idea
body: Fixed and mildly critical: too attached to something to give it up. Also wedded bliss, where wedded is just an adjective. (быть приверженным (идее), держаться за)
examples: She has wedded herself to a theory the data doesn't support.
He is too wedded to the old process to see the problem.

entries.forms: wed /wɛd/ · wed /wɛd/ or wedded /ˈwɛdɪd/ · wed /wɛd/ or wedded /ˈwɛdɪd/
entries.register: dated — survives in headlines and in wedded to; Americans say get married
entries.third person: weds · -ing form: wedding (the d doubles — same spelling as the noun wedding)
entries.contrast: Both forms are standard American. Wed is what headlines use — Couple weds after 40 years — while wedded survives mostly as an adjective: wedded bliss, wedded to the idea. In plain speech Americans say got married.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; dated outside headlines, and wedded survives mainly as an adjective (wedded bliss, too wedded to the old process).
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive of the couple (they wed in a courthouse ceremony last fall), transitive of the officiant or of joining two things (the same judge wed both of my sisters, a good design weds comfort to durability).
entries.passive: restricted — the officiant sense passivizes (half the couples in that town have been wedded by a retired chaplain) but sounds archaic; be wedded to an idea is the adjective, not a passive.

entries.meaning: To make something wet, including the polite way of saying someone urinated.
examples: Wet the brush before you load the paint.
Rain has wet the whole stack of newspapers.
Someone had wet the sponge and left it on the counter.
He wets his hair down before every interview.
The technician wetted the slide with a drop of saline.
The toddler wet the bed twice last week.
He laughed so hard he nearly wet himself.
The puppy has wet the rug again.
They stopped at a tavern to wet their whistles.
He had wet his whistle before the speech, and it showed.

senses.head: Make something wet
body: American English prefers the invariant wet; wetted turns up in technical writing (the wetted surface) and is the usual British choice. (мочить, смачивать, увлажнять)
examples: Wet the brush before you load the paint.
Rain has wet the whole stack of newspapers.
Someone had wet the sponge and left it on the counter.
He wets his hair down before every interview.
The technician wetted the slide with a drop of saline.

senses.head: Urinate on or in something
body: The polite way to say it: wet the bed, wet oneself, wet his pants. (мочиться, описаться)
examples: The toddler wet the bed twice last week.
He laughed so hard he nearly wet himself.
The puppy has wet the rug again.

senses.head: wet one's whistle
body: A dated, jokey idiom for having a drink. (промочить горло, выпить)
examples: They stopped at a tavern to wet their whistles.
He had wet his whistle before the speech, and it showed.

entries.forms: wet /wɛt/ · wet /wɛt/ or wetted /ˈwɛtɪd/ · wet /wɛt/ or wetted /ˈwɛtɪd/
entries.register: everyday — ordinary for wetting a cloth, a brush, or the bed
entries.contrast: Both forms are standard. American English prefers the invariant wet — the baby wet the bed — while wetted is used in technical writing (the wetted surface) and is the usual British choice. Note that wet is far commoner as an adjective than as a verb.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and far commoner as an adjective than as a verb.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is what gets wet, often reflexive or a fixed noun (wet the brush, he nearly wet himself, the toddler wet the bed).
entries.passive: yes — the slide was wetted with a drop of saline, the whole stack of newspapers has been wet by the rain — though in speech people say got wet.
